title: CFS/EEVDF scheduler & preemption models
tldr: Since 6.6, SCHED_NORMAL tasks are picked by EEVDF instead of CFS's pure min-vruntime rule; the preemption model decides where running kernel code can be preempted.
body: Linux schedules through scheduling classes checked in priority order: stop, deadline (SCHED_DEADLINE), realtime (SCHED_FIFO/SCHED_RR), fair (SCHED_NORMAL, SCHED_BATCH, SCHED_IDLE), then idle; 6.12 added the optional sched_ext class for BPF-defined schedulers, sitting below fair. Each CPU has a struct rq with per-class sub-queues. schedule() calls pick_next_task(), which asks each class in turn, then context_switch() switches the memory context and register state. The fair class still lives in kernel/sched/fair.c.

CFS tracked a per-entity vruntime: real runtime scaled by load weight (nice 0 = 1024, each nice step roughly a 1.25x weight ratio, about 10% CPU), and always ran the entity with the smallest vruntime from a red-black tree. EEVDF, merged in 6.6, keeps weighted fair sharing but adds lag (service owed minus service received) and a virtual deadline (vruntime plus the requested slice scaled by weight). Among eligible entities (lag >= 0) it runs the one with the earliest virtual deadline, so a task asking for shorter slices gets on the CPU sooner, but not more CPU in total.

The preemption model controls preemption of kernel-mode code; user space is always preemptible. PREEMPT_NONE switches only when kernel code blocks, returns to user space or calls cond_resched(). PREEMPT_VOLUNTARY also turns might_sleep() annotations into rescheduling points. PREEMPT (full) allows preemption anywhere preempt_count is zero. PREEMPT_RT, mainline since 6.12, also makes most spinlocks sleepable. PREEMPT_DYNAMIC lets you choose at boot with preempt=, and 6.13 added PREEMPT_LAZY, which defers preemption of fair tasks to the next tick or return to user space.

Mechanically, preemption is requested by setting TIF_NEED_RESCHED on the running task, from the scheduler tick or when a wakeup produces a more deserving task. The flag is acted on at return to user space, at interrupt exit if the interrupted kernel code is preemptible, and at preempt_enable() when the count drops to zero. Real-time classes are not fair at all: a runnable SCHED_FIFO task always beats every fair task on that CPU.
diagram:
schedule() -> pick_next_task(): ask classes in order
 +------+  +----------+  +----+  +------+  +-----+  +------+
 | stop |->| deadline |->| rt |->| fair |->| ext |->| idle |
 +------+  +----------+  +----+  +------+  +-----+  +------+
                                    |   (ext: 6.12+, optional)
 fair class (EEVDF, 6.6+):
   lag      = service owed - service received
   eligible = lag >= 0
   deadline = vruntime + slice * NICE_0_LOAD / weight
   pick the eligible entity with the earliest deadline
keypoints: Class order: stop > deadline > rt > fair (> ext) > idle; RT priorities 1-99 always beat SCHED_NORMAL.
EEVDF replaced CFS's pick rule in 6.6; vruntime and load weights remain, plus lag and virtual deadlines.
Nice 0 has weight 1024; one nice step is roughly a 10% CPU-share difference (weight ratio ~1.25).
Preemption is requested via TIF_NEED_RESCHED and taken at return-to-user, IRQ exit (if preemptible) or preempt_enable().
Models: none, voluntary, full, lazy (6.13), RT (mainline 6.12); PREEMPT_DYNAMIC selects at boot with preempt=.

interview.q: What does preempt_count track?
interview.a: A counter (per-CPU on x86, in thread_info elsewhere) with fields for preempt_disable() nesting, softirq/BH-disable count, hardirq nesting and NMI. Kernel code may be preempted or sleep only when it is zero. in_interrupt(), in_softirq() and in_atomic() read these bits. On non-RT kernels spin_lock() raises it, which is why sleeping under a spinlock produces 'BUG: scheduling while atomic'.

interview.q: How do SCHED_FIFO and SCHED_RR differ?
interview.a: Both are fixed-priority realtime policies with priorities 1-99 that preempt any fair task. A SCHED_FIFO task runs until it blocks, yields or a higher-priority task becomes runnable. SCHED_RR adds a timeslice (sched_rr_timeslice_ms, 100 ms by default) so equal-priority RR tasks rotate. A runaway FIFO task can starve a CPU, which is why RT throttling and, in recent kernels, a fair deadline server reserve some time for normal tasks.

interview.q: Why did EEVDF replace CFS?
interview.a: CFS delivered fair shares but had no way to express latency needs; it relied on heuristics such as sleeper credit and wakeup-granularity tunables. EEVDF gives a principled rule: lag maintains fairness, and virtual deadlines order eligible tasks, so a task requesting shorter slices runs sooner and more often but not for more total time. It removed several heuristics, and recent kernels let a task request a custom slice through sched_setattr().

pitfalls: Saying CFS is still the algorithm in 6.6+: the fair class remains, but it picks by EEVDF.
Treating nice values as strict priorities; they are weights, and a nice 19 task still gets some CPU.
Confusing kernel preemption (CONFIG_PREEMPT*) with user-space preemption, which always exists.

title: sk_buff lifecycle
tldr: struct sk_buff is the packet's metadata descriptor; its head, data, tail and end pointers let each layer add or strip headers without copying, from allocation to consume_skb().
body: struct sk_buff holds metadata only; packet bytes live in a separate buffer. Four pointers frame the linear area: head (buffer start), data (start of the current layer), tail (end of data) and end (where struct skb_shared_info begins); on 64-bit, tail and end are stored as offsets. skb->len is the total length; skb->data_len is the part held in paged fragments (skb_shinfo(skb)->frags[]) or the frag_list chain, so the linear length is len minus data_len. Header positions are kept in mac_header, network_header and transport_header.

Header handling is pointer arithmetic: skb_reserve() creates headroom in an empty skb, skb_put() extends tail to append data, skb_push() moves data back to prepend a header on TX, and skb_pull() moves data forward to strip one on RX. pskb_may_pull() guarantees enough bytes are linear before parsing a header, pulling them from fragments if needed. skb->cb[48] is a scratch area owned by whichever layer currently holds the skb, for example TCP_SKB_CB().

On RX a driver allocates with napi_alloc_skb() or wraps a page_pool buffer with napi_build_skb(), sets protocol via eth_type_trans(), checksum status and hash, and passes it up. On TX the socket layer allocates the skb with headroom for all lower headers. skb_clone() creates a new sk_buff sharing the data buffer (refcounted through dataref); skb_copy()/pskb_copy() duplicate data; skb_cow_head() or skb_unshare() come before writing into a buffer that may be shared.

Freeing records the outcome. consume_skb() is for normal completion; kfree_skb() and kfree_skb_reason() are for drops and fire the skb:kfree_skb tracepoint with a drop reason (5.17+), which dropwatch, perf and pwru use. Drivers freeing TX skbs from arbitrary context use dev_kfree_skb_any(), and NAPI poll uses napi_consume_skb() to batch-recycle heads. sk_buff structs come from a dedicated slab cache with per-CPU NAPI caches on top.
diagram:
head     data                  tail      end
  |        |                     |         |
  v        v                     v         v
  +--------+---------------------+---------+------------+
  |headroom| linear data         |tailroom | shinfo:    |
  |        | (len - data_len)    |         | frags[],   |
  +--------+---------------------+---------+ frag_list  |
                                           +------------+
 skb_push(): data moves left    skb_put(): tail moves right
 skb_pull(): data moves right   skb_reserve(): data+tail right
 skb->len = linear bytes + skb->data_len (paged/frag_list)
keypoints: sk_buff is metadata; the data buffer is separate, with skb_shared_info at its end.
skb_reserve/put/push/pull adjust pointers; headers are added and stripped without copying.
len includes paged data; data_len is the non-linear part; call pskb_may_pull() before parsing.
skb_clone() shares data read-only; copy or skb_cow*() before modifying.
consume_skb() for success, kfree_skb_reason() for drops (visible to drop monitors).

interview.q: Why is headroom reserved?
interview.a: So lower layers can prepend headers with skb_push() without reallocating. TCP allocates with MAX_TCP_HEADER of headroom, enough for TCP, IP and link-layer headers. Devices needing more, for tunnels or in-band hardware metadata, declare needed_headroom on the net_device, and skb_cow_head() reallocates if headroom is short. On RX, NET_SKB_PAD plus NET_IP_ALIGN keeps the IP header aligned after the 14-byte Ethernet header.

interview.q: What is the difference between skb_clone() and skb_copy()?
interview.a: skb_clone() allocates a new sk_buff that points at the same data buffer and bumps its dataref count; it is cheap and used when two consumers need the packet, such as a packet tap and the stack. Neither side may modify the shared data. skb_copy() duplicates the header and all data into a new linear buffer; pskb_copy() copies only the linear part and shares fragments. TCP clones on transmit so the original stays queued for retransmission.

interview.q: What are paged fragments for?
interview.a: They let an skb reference data in pages without copying it into the linear area: GRO-merged segments, sendfile and splice pages, NIC buffers from page_pool. Up to MAX_SKB_FRAGS page descriptors (17 by default, a Kconfig option in recent kernels) live in skb_shared_info. Devices handle them via scatter-gather (NETIF_F_SG); if a device cannot, the stack linearises the skb before transmit.

pitfalls: Thinking skb->len is only the linear length; it includes fragments.
Writing into a cloned skb's data without skb_unshare() or skb_cow*().
Parsing headers directly from skb->data without pskb_may_pull(), reading past the linear area.

title: Boot flow: ROM, SPL, U-Boot, kernel, init
tldr: BootROM loads a small first stage into SRAM, SPL or TF-A initialises DRAM, U-Boot loads kernel, DTB and initramfs, and the kernel finally starts PID 1.
body: On power-up the SoC executes its mask ROM (BootROM). It reads boot-mode pins or fuses, initialises a minimal boot device (eMMC boot partition, SD, SPI NOR, NAND, or USB/UART recovery) and loads a small first-stage image into on-chip SRAM, because DRAM is not configured yet. With secure boot enabled, the ROM verifies that image's signature against a key hash burned into OTP fuses before jumping to it.

The first-stage loader, U-Boot SPL or TF-A BL2 on many arm64 parts, sets up clocks, the PMIC and the DRAM controller (including training for DDR4 or LPDDR4), then loads the next stage into DRAM. A typical arm64 chain is BL2, then BL31 (the TF-A EL3 runtime providing PSCI for CPU on/off and suspend), an optional BL32 (OP-TEE), then BL33, which is U-Boot proper running at EL2 or EL1. On 32-bit ARM, SPL usually loads U-Boot directly.

U-Boot initialises storage and networking, reads its environment and loads the kernel Image (arm64) or zImage (arm32), a DTB and optionally an initramfs, often packed in a FIT image with hashes and signatures. It fixes up the DT (/chosen/bootargs, memory, MAC addresses) and jumps with booti, bootz or bootm. The arm64 boot protocol requires the MMU off, the kernel image cleaned to the point of coherency, and the DTB physical address in x0; arm32 passes it in r2.

The kernel's head.S builds early page tables and enables the MMU, then start_kernel() sets up memory, the scheduler, interrupts and timers, unflattens the DT and runs initcalls, which probe drivers. kernel_init() unpacks the initramfs and executes its /init if present; otherwise it mounts root= and runs /sbin/init (or init=) as PID 1, typically systemd or BusyBox init. Failures here produce the familiar 'VFS: Unable to mount root fs' or 'No working init found' panics.
diagram:
power on -> BootROM: boot pins/fuses, 1st stage to SRAM
   |
 SPL / TF-A BL2: clocks, PMIC, DRAM init + training
   |
 (arm64) BL31 EL3 runtime, PSCI -> [BL32 OP-TEE]
   |
 U-Boot proper (BL33): load Image + DTB + initramfs (FIT)
   |  booti: x0 = DTB address, MMU off
 Linux head.S -> start_kernel() -> initcalls, probe
   |
 kernel_init(): /init from initramfs, or root= /sbin/init
   |
 PID 1 (systemd / BusyBox init) -> user space
keypoints: ROM -> SPL/BL2 (DRAM init) -> [BL31/BL32] -> U-Boot -> kernel -> init.
SPL exists because DRAM is not usable at reset; it runs from on-chip SRAM.
arm64: DTB address in x0 with the MMU off; arm32: DTB address in r2.
bootargs reach the kernel through /chosen in the DTB.
Secure boot: ROM verifies the first stage via a fused key hash; each stage verifies the next (e.g. signed FIT).

interview.q: Why can't the BootROM load U-Boot directly?
interview.a: Full U-Boot is hundreds of KiB to over a MiB and expects DRAM, but at reset only on-chip SRAM is available, often 64 to 256 KiB, and the ROM knows nothing about the board's DRAM type or timings. SPL is small enough to fit in SRAM and contains the board-specific DRAM and PMIC initialisation. SoCs with large SRAM or ROM-driven DRAM setup can skip it.

interview.q: How do you debug a board that hangs right after 'Starting kernel ...'?
interview.a: Usually the kernel is running but has no console. Enable earlycon (a stdout-path in the DT plus 'earlycon', or an explicit earlycon=uart8250,mmio32,ADDR), and on arm32 consider CONFIG_DEBUG_LL. Check console=, that the DTB matches the kernel, that kernel, DTB and initramfs load addresses do not overlap, and that the kernel was built for the right platform. A JTAG probe can dump the printk buffer from RAM.

interview.q: What does the initramfs do?
interview.a: It is a cpio archive, usually compressed, that the kernel unpacks into a tmpfs-backed rootfs. If it contains /init, that runs as PID 1. It loads drivers needed for the real root (storage, crypto, LVM), assembles or decrypts it, then switch_root moves to it. Small embedded systems may run entirely from the initramfs. It replaced the older initrd, which was a block-device image.

pitfalls: Saying the kernel initialises DRAM; the boot loader does.
Booting with a DTB from a different kernel version or board.
Loading the DTB or initramfs where the kernel will decompress or relocate itself.

title: Process vs thread & task_struct
tldr: Linux has one task_struct per thread; a process is a thread group whose tasks share mm, files and signal handlers, chosen by clone() flags.
body: The kernel has no separate thread object: every schedulable entity is a struct task_struct. Processes and threads differ only in what they share, chosen by clone() flags. fork() shares nothing and copies memory copy-on-write. glibc's pthread_create() calls clone3() or clone() with CLONE_VM, CLONE_FS, CLONE_FILES, CLONE_SIGHAND, CLONE_THREAD, CLONE_SYSVSEM and TLS/TID flags, so the threads share mm_struct, files_struct, fs_struct and sighand_struct. All variants converge in kernel_clone() and copy_process().

The naming is confusing: the kernel's task->pid is per task and is what user space calls the thread ID (gettid()), while task->tgid is the thread group ID, which getpid() returns. The first thread's TID equals the TGID. A signal sent to a process targets the whole thread group and is delivered to any thread that does not block it; tgkill() targets one thread. /proc/PID/task/ lists the threads. If the group leader exits early, it stays a zombie until every thread has exited.

task_struct holds scheduling state (__state, prio, and the se, rt and dl entities), memory (mm, active_mm), credentials (cred), open files, signal state, namespaces (nsproxy), cgroup membership and process-tree links. Each task has a kernel stack (16 KiB on x86-64 and arm64, usually vmap'd with guard pages under CONFIG_VMAP_STACK) and architecture state in thread_struct. current yields the running task cheaply: a per-CPU variable on x86, the sp_el0 register on arm64.

States: TASK_RUNNING (running or queued), TASK_INTERRUPTIBLE (sleeping, woken by signals, 'S' in ps), TASK_UNINTERRUPTIBLE ('D', counted in the load average), TASK_KILLABLE (uninterruptible except for fatal signals), stopped and traced, and the exit states EXIT_ZOMBIE (waiting for the parent's wait()) and EXIT_DEAD. Kernel threads (kthread_create()) have mm == NULL and borrow the previous task's active_mm, avoiding a page-table switch.
diagram:
process A (TGID 100)               process B (TGID 200)
 +-----------------------------+    +------------------+
 | task pid=100   task pid=101 |    | task pid=200     |
 |  (leader)       (thread)    |    |                  |
 +------|--------------|-------+    +--------|---------+
        +------+-------+                     |
               v                             v
   shared: mm_struct, files_struct,   own mm_struct (COW
   fs_struct, sighand_struct          copy after fork),
                                      own files_struct
 getpid() returns tgid: 100 in both threads of A
 gettid() returns pid:  100 and 101
keypoints: One task_struct per thread; threads are tasks sharing mm, files, fs and sighand via CLONE_* flags.
getpid() returns the TGID; gettid() returns the per-task PID.
fork/vfork/clone/clone3 -> kernel_clone() -> copy_process(); memory is copy-on-write after fork.
Kernel threads have mm == NULL and borrow active_mm.
D state = TASK_UNINTERRUPTIBLE, counted in load average; zombies wait to be reaped by wait().

interview.q: What happens to other threads when one thread calls execve()?
interview.a: execve() kills every other thread in the group (de_thread()); if a non-leader called it, that thread takes over the leader's PID. The new program starts with a single thread, a fresh address space and signal handlers reset to default, while descriptors without close-on-exec stay open. So exec in a multithreaded program abruptly ends all other threads.

interview.q: What is vfork() and why is it faster than fork()?
interview.a: vfork() creates a child that shares the parent's memory (CLONE_VM | CLONE_VFORK) and suspends the parent until the child calls execve() or _exit(). No page tables are copied, so it stays fast even for huge processes. The child must not modify memory or return from the calling function. glibc's posix_spawn() uses clone with CLONE_VM | CLONE_VFORK internally to get the same benefit safely.

interview.q: Why can't you kill a process in D state?
interview.a: TASK_UNINTERRUPTIBLE sleeps ignore signals, including SIGKILL, because the code waiting, often for I/O or a lock, cannot safely abort. The signal stays pending and is acted on when the task wakes. Long D states usually mean stuck I/O, such as NFS or a failing disk, or a driver bug; the hung-task detector warns after 120 s by default. TASK_KILLABLE waits, such as mutex_lock_killable(), let fatal signals through.

pitfalls: Saying Linux threads use a different kernel structure from processes.
Mixing up PID, TID and TGID: getpid() in any thread returns the TGID.
Thinking fork() copies all memory immediately.

title: Virtual memory, page tables & page faults
tldr: Each process has an mm_struct of VMAs plus a multi-level page table; the MMU walks the tables and page faults let the kernel populate mappings lazily.
body: A process address space is a struct mm_struct: a set of vm_area_struct regions (kept in a maple tree since 6.1) plus a page-table root, mm->pgd. VMAs describe what may be mapped and with which permissions; page tables describe what is mapped right now. Generic code uses five levels, PGD, P4D, PUD, PMD and PTE, folded at compile time when the architecture has fewer. x86-64 uses 4 levels (48-bit VA) or 5 with LA57 (57-bit); arm64 with 4 KiB pages uses 4 levels for a 48-bit VA.

On a TLB miss the MMU walks the tables in hardware (x86, arm64). A missing or permission-violating entry raises a page fault. On x86, exc_page_fault() leads to do_user_addr_fault(), which finds the VMA (locklessly with per-VMA locks since 6.4, falling back to mmap_lock) and calls handle_mm_fault(). That walks or allocates table levels and dispatches: do_anonymous_page() for first touch of anonymous memory, do_fault() for file-backed pages, do_wp_page() for copy-on-write and do_swap_page() for swapped-out pages.

A minor fault is resolved without I/O (zero page, page already in the page cache, COW copy); a major fault needs I/O. No VMA or wrong permissions gives SIGSEGV; touching a file mapping beyond end-of-file gives SIGBUS. Kernel-mode faults on user addresses are allowed only at instructions with exception-table entries, i.e. inside copy_from_user() and friends. Kernel memory is mostly mapped up front: the linear (direct) map covers RAM, while vmalloc and ioremap ranges get their own entries.

Changing or removing a PTE requires TLB invalidation: local flushes plus IPIs on x86, or broadcast TLBI instructions on arm64, for every CPU that may cache the entry. ASIDs (arm64) and PCIDs (x86) tag TLB entries per address space so a context switch need not flush everything. Huge pages (2 MiB at PMD level, 1 GiB at PUD level on x86-64, via hugetlbfs or transparent huge pages) reduce TLB pressure and page-walk depth.
diagram:
x86-64, 4 KiB pages, 4-level paging (48-bit VA)
 47     39 38     30 29     21 20     12 11          0
 +---------+---------+---------+---------+------------+
 | PGD idx | PUD idx | PMD idx | PTE idx |   offset   |
 +---------+---------+---------+---------+------------+
   9 bits    9 bits    9 bits    9 bits     12 bits

 CR3 -> PGD[i] -> PUD[j] -> PMD[k] -> PTE[l] -> page + off
 (P4D folded away unless 5-level/LA57 is enabled)
 missing/invalid entry -> #PF -> handle_mm_fault()
keypoints: VMAs = what is allowed; page tables = what is currently mapped.
Levels PGD -> P4D -> PUD -> PMD -> PTE, folded per architecture; 9 index bits per level on x86-64 with 4 KiB pages.
Fault path: arch handler -> handle_mm_fault() -> anonymous / file / COW / swap handlers.
Minor fault = no I/O, major fault = I/O; no VMA -> SIGSEGV, beyond EOF of a file mapping -> SIGBUS.
VMAs live in a maple tree (6.1); per-VMA locks (6.4) avoid mmap_lock on most faults.

interview.q: What happens to memory on fork()?
interview.a: copy_process() duplicates the mm via dup_mm(): VMAs are copied, and for private writable mappings the PTEs are copied read-only in both parent and child, sharing the same physical pages with raised refcounts. The first write by either side faults into do_wp_page(), which copies the page (or reuses it if it is no longer shared) and maps it writable. Shared mappings stay shared. If exec() follows, the copy is thrown away.

interview.q: What is a TLB shootdown and why is it expensive?
interview.a: When the kernel changes or removes a PTE that other CPUs may hold in their TLBs, those entries must be invalidated. On x86 that means IPIs to the CPUs in the mm's cpumask and waiting for them to flush; arm64 can broadcast TLBI instructions in hardware. munmap, mprotect, page migration and reclaim all trigger it. Batching flushes and lazy-TLB mode for kernel threads reduce the cost.

interview.q: How does the kernel safely access user memory?
interview.a: Through copy_from_user(), copy_to_user(), get_user() and put_user(). They check that the range is a user address (access_ok()), temporarily lift SMAP/PAN, and perform the access at instructions listed in the exception table, so a fault on an unmapped address returns -EFAULT instead of oopsing. Dereferencing a __user pointer directly is a bug that sparse flags and SMAP/PAN trap at runtime.

pitfalls: Saying malloc() allocates physical memory; it reserves virtual space and pages arrive on first touch.
Treating every page fault as an error; most are normal demand-paging or COW faults.
Assuming kernel memory faults in lazily like user memory; a kernel-mode fault outside exception-table sites oopses.

title: NAPI & interrupt mitigation
tldr: NAPI switches a NIC from interrupt-per-packet to budgeted polling in NET_RX_SOFTIRQ under load, preventing receive livelock; hardware coalescing further trades latency for fewer interrupts.
body: An interrupt per packet collapses under load: at millions of packets per second the CPU spends its time entering and leaving IRQ handlers while the code that would consume packets starves, which is receive livelock. NAPI switches to polling. The driver's IRQ handler masks the queue's interrupt and calls napi_schedule(), which puts the napi_struct on the per-CPU poll list and raises NET_RX_SOFTIRQ. net_rx_action() then calls the driver's poll(napi, budget) callback.

poll() cleans TX completions, processes up to budget RX packets (the weight, normally 64), builds skbs and feeds them to napi_gro_receive(). If it did less work than the budget, the ring is empty: it calls napi_complete_done() and, if that returns true, re-enables the interrupt. If it used the whole budget it returns budget and stays on the poll list. net_rx_action() bounds each round by netdev_budget (300 packets) and netdev_budget_usecs (2 ms), then leaves the remainder to ksoftirqd.

Hardware coalescing complements NAPI: ethtool -C eth0 rx-usecs 50 rx-frames 32 delays interrupts so each one covers more packets, trading latency for throughput, and adaptive modes tune this automatically. Software knobs gro_flush_timeout and napi_defer_hard_irqs keep polling instead of re-arming interrupts. Threaded NAPI (write 1 to /sys/class/net/eth0/threaded) runs poll in a per-NAPI kthread you can pin and prioritise, and SO_BUSY_POLL lets a socket poll the queue directly for minimum latency.

Modern NICs have one NAPI instance per queue (or RX/TX queue pair), each with its own MSI-X vector, so RSS spreads flows over CPUs and each queue is polled on the CPU that took its interrupt. Registration is netif_napi_add() (the weight argument was dropped in 6.1) followed by napi_enable(); teardown is napi_disable() then netif_napi_del().
diagram:
packet -> NIC DMA into RX ring -> MSI-X interrupt
                                       |
 driver IRQ handler: mask queue IRQ, napi_schedule()
                                       |
                            raise NET_RX_SOFTIRQ
                                       |
 net_rx_action(): for each napi on the poll list
   work = driver_poll(napi, budget = 64)
     work < budget : napi_complete_done(), unmask IRQ
     work == budget: stay on poll list, poll again
 per round: netdev_budget = 300, netdev_budget_usecs = 2000
 still busy -> ksoftirqd/N continues the work
keypoints: IRQ handler: mask the device/queue interrupt and napi_schedule(); real work happens in NET_RX_SOFTIRQ.
poll() returns work done; below budget -> napi_complete_done() and re-enable the IRQ.
Default weight 64; per-round limits netdev_budget (300) and netdev_budget_usecs (2000).
TX completion cleaning happens in poll and does not count against the RX budget.
Tunables: ethtool -C coalescing, gro_flush_timeout, napi_defer_hard_irqs, threaded NAPI, busy polling.

interview.q: What is receive livelock and how does NAPI prevent it?
interview.a: Under heavy load an interrupt-per-packet driver spends all CPU time in hardirq handlers, which preempt the softirq and user-space processing that would actually consume packets, so useful throughput falls towards zero. NAPI keeps RX interrupts off while work remains and polls with a bounded budget, so excess packets are dropped in the NIC ring before costing CPU, and other work keeps running.

interview.q: What does napi_complete_done()'s return value mean?
interview.a: It returns false when NAPI must keep polling: busy polling currently owns the instance, IRQ deferral via napi_defer_hard_irqs armed a timer instead, or an interrupt raced in and set NAPI_STATE_MISSED, in which case the core reschedules the poll. Drivers re-enable the device interrupt only when it returns true; otherwise they would re-arm an IRQ while polling continues.

interview.q: How does RSS relate to NAPI?
interview.a: RSS hashes packet headers in the NIC, typically the 4-tuple with a Toeplitz hash, to choose one of several RX queues, each with its own MSI-X vector and NAPI instance. Spreading IRQ affinity across CPUs makes softirq processing scale. RPS is the software equivalent for NICs with too few queues, and RFS or accelerated RFS steer each flow to the CPU where its consuming application runs.

pitfalls: Processing packets in the hardirq handler instead of in poll().
Calling napi_complete_done() when the full budget was consumed, or returning budget after completing.
Assuming interrupt coalescing only affects throughput; it adds latency directly.

title: Device tree: compatible, reg, interrupts, overlays
tldr: A device tree describes non-discoverable hardware; compatible picks the driver, reg and interrupts are decoded by parent cell counts, and overlays patch the tree for add-on hardware.
body: A device tree describes hardware that cannot be discovered: CPUs, memory, buses, peripherals and how they are wired. Sources (.dts, sharing .dtsi includes) are compiled by dtc into a flattened blob (.dtb) that the boot loader passes to the kernel. The kernel unflattens it into struct device_nodes, and of_platform_populate() creates platform devices for nodes under simple buses. It describes hardware, not policy; bindings in Documentation/devicetree/bindings are YAML schemas checked with make dtbs_check.

compatible is a list from most to least specific, e.g. "acme,soc2-uart", "acme,soc1-uart"; drivers match it through of_device_id tables, so a new SoC can reuse an older driver. reg lists address and size pairs whose cell counts come from the parent's #address-cells and #size-cells: for MMIO it is the register window, for an I2C child a single cell holding the 7-bit address with #size-cells of 0. status = "okay" enables a node, while "disabled" keeps it from being probed.

interrupts is decoded by the node's interrupt-parent (inherited when absent) according to that controller's #interrupt-cells. For an ARM GIC that is three cells: type (GIC_SPI = 0 or GIC_PPI = 1), number (SPI n is interrupt ID n + 32), and trigger flags such as IRQ_TYPE_LEVEL_HIGH = 4. For a GPIO controller acting as interrupt controller it is usually pin and flags. interrupts-extended names a parent per entry. Other links use phandles: clocks, resets, pinctrl-0, *-gpios, dmas, each decoded by its provider's cells property.

Overlays (.dtbo) patch a base tree for add-on boards or FPGA designs. The base must be built with symbols (dtc -@) so overlay fragments can reference its labels, such as &i2c1. They are usually applied by the boot loader, for example U-Boot's fdt apply. The kernel offers of_overlay_fdt_apply() for in-kernel users, but mainline has no general user-space interface for runtime overlays; the configfs interface remains out of tree.
keypoints: compatible: most specific first; matched against of_device_id tables.
reg cell counts come from the parent's #address-cells / #size-cells.
interrupts are decoded by the interrupt-parent's #interrupt-cells (GIC: type, number, flags; SPI n = ID n + 32).
status "okay" / "disabled"; phandles link clocks, resets, GPIOs, pinctrl and DMA.
Overlays need a base DTB built with -@ and are usually applied by the boot loader.

interview.q: Why list several compatible strings?
interview.a: The first names the exact hardware so a driver can apply quirks; later entries name older IP that the block is compatible with, so a kernel without a driver for the new string still binds through the fallback. The OF matching code scores matches, preferring entries earlier in the node's list. Never invent a generic compatible like "uart"; always use a vendor,part string.

interview.q: How does a driver read custom properties?
interview.a: With of_property_read_u32(), of_property_read_string() and similar helpers or, preferably, the firmware-agnostic device_property_read_u32() family, which also works with ACPI _DSD. For GPIOs use devm_gpiod_get() rather than legacy of_get_named_gpio(). Optional properties should fall back to sensible defaults when absent, and any new property needs a binding schema update reviewed by the DT maintainers.

interview.q: What is the difference between device tree and ACPI?
interview.a: Both describe non-discoverable hardware to the OS. DT is static data; ACPI tables also contain AML bytecode that the OS executes for methods such as power control, so firmware stays involved at runtime. DT dominates embedded ARM, RISC-V and PowerPC; ACPI is standard on x86 and on arm64 servers. Linux's fwnode and device_property APIs let one driver support both.

pitfalls: Encoding software policy in the DT instead of describing hardware, which DT reviewers reject.
Getting reg wrong because the parent's #address-cells/#size-cells differ from what you assumed.
Writing the GIC interrupt ID (n + 32) where the binding expects the SPI number.

title: Memory layout of a process (text/data/bss/heap/stack)
tldr: A process has text, rodata, data and bss from the ELF file, a brk heap, an mmap area for libraries and anonymous memory, and a downward-growing stack, randomised by ASLR.
body: A typical Linux user address space, from low to high: the ELF segments (text r-x, rodata r--, data and bss rw-), then the heap growing upward from the program break, a large region where mmap() places shared libraries, file and anonymous mappings and thread stacks (allocated top-down below the stack area on x86-64), and finally the main thread's stack near the top, growing downward. The vDSO and vvar pages sit among the mappings. /proc/self/maps shows all of it.

.text holds machine code and .rodata string literals and const data. .data holds initialised globals and statics, with their values stored in the file; .bss holds zero-initialised and uninitialised globals and statics, takes no file space, and is mapped as zero-filled memory. size a.out reports the three. Locals live on the stack or only in registers, while static locals live in data or bss. String literals are read-only, so writing through char *p = "abc" is undefined and usually segfaults.

glibc malloc() serves small requests from arenas grown with brk() (main arena) or mmap'ed heaps (other arenas), and large ones, above a threshold starting at 128 KiB and adjusted dynamically, directly with mmap(), so free() returns those immediately. All of this reserves virtual memory; physical pages arrive on first touch, subject to overcommit policy (vm.overcommit_memory). The main stack is limited by RLIMIT_STACK (commonly 8 MiB) and grows on fault, protected by a guard gap; thread stacks are fixed-size mappings with guard pages.

ASLR (/proc/sys/kernel/randomize_va_space, 2 by default) randomises the stack, mmap base, vDSO, heap start and, for PIE executables, the text base. On x86-64 with 4-level paging user space spans the lower 128 TiB (TASK_SIZE just under 0x0000800000000000), the kernel occupies the upper canonical half, and user-mode accesses to kernel addresses fault. 32-bit x86 kernels traditionally split 3 GiB for user and 1 GiB for the kernel.
diagram:
high  ~0x7ffffffff000 (x86-64, 4-level)
       +---------------------------+
       | stack (main thread)    v  |  RLIMIT_STACK
       +---------------------------+
       | mmap area              v  |  libs, anon, thread
       |   ... unmapped gap ...    |  stacks
       | heap (brk)             ^  |  small malloc chunks
       +---------------------------+
       | .bss    zero-init globals |  no space in file
       | .data   initialised data  |
       | .rodata consts, literals  |
       | .text   code (r-x)        |
 low   +---------------------------+  PIE base randomised
keypoints: text (r-x), rodata, data (initialised), bss (zeroed, no file space), heap (brk), mmap area, stack (grows down).
glibc malloc: brk/arenas for small requests, mmap for large ones (threshold starts at 128 KiB).
Virtual reservation is not physical memory; pages are allocated on first touch.
Main stack limited by RLIMIT_STACK (often 8 MiB); thread stacks are mmaps with guard pages.
ASLR randomises stack, mmap, heap, vDSO and PIE text; /proc/PID/maps shows the layout.

interview.q: Where do these live: global int a; static int b = 5; const char *s = "hi"; and a local int c?
interview.a: a is an uninitialised global, so .bss. b is an initialised static, so .data. s is an initialised, non-const pointer, so it lives in .data (with a relocation in a PIE), while the literal "hi" lives in .rodata. c has automatic storage: it is on the stack or only in a register, not in any section. Static storage is always zero-initialised unless given a value.

interview.q: Why doesn't RSS drop after free()?
interview.a: glibc returns memory to the kernel only when it can. Large mmap'ed chunks are unmapped immediately, but brk-heap memory is released only from the top of the heap beyond the trim threshold, and live chunks pin the pages around them. Freed chunks are kept in bins for reuse. malloc_trim() can release free pages in the middle of the heap with madvise(MADV_DONTNEED). jemalloc and tcmalloc behave differently.

interview.q: What happens on a stack overflow?
interview.a: The stack grows on page faults until it hits RLIMIT_STACK or the guard gap next to another mapping (stack_guard_gap, 256 pages by default since the 2017 Stack Clash fixes). Then the fault cannot be satisfied and the process gets SIGSEGV, which a handler can catch only on an alternate signal stack (sigaltstack). In the kernel, VMAP_STACK puts guard pages around kernel stacks, so overflow oopses instead of silently corrupting memory.

pitfalls: Saying uninitialised globals contain garbage; static storage is zero-initialised (bss).
Confusing virtual size (VSZ) with resident memory (RSS).
Modifying string literals.

title: kmalloc vs vmalloc vs slab & GFP flags
tldr: kmalloc returns physically contiguous slab memory, vmalloc returns virtually contiguous pages, kmem_cache serves fixed-size objects, and GFP flags say whether the allocator may sleep.
body: At the bottom is the buddy page allocator: alloc_pages(gfp, order) returns 2^order physically contiguous pages, typically up to order 10 (4 MiB with 4 KiB pages), from zones such as ZONE_DMA, ZONE_DMA32 and ZONE_NORMAL. The slab allocator carves pages into objects; since 6.8 SLUB is the only implementation (SLOB went in 6.4, SLAB in 6.8). kmem_cache_create() makes a dedicated cache for a frequently allocated struct, with per-CPU slabs making the fast path lockless.

kmalloc() fronts a set of generic size-class caches (kmalloc-8 up to kmalloc-8k with 4 KiB pages); larger requests go straight to the page allocator. The memory is physically contiguous and in the direct map, so virt_to_phys() works and it can be DMA-mapped. Requests round up to a size class, so kmalloc(1100) consumes 2048 bytes. In drivers prefer kzalloc(), overflow-checked kcalloc(), and devm_kzalloc() for binding-scoped lifetime. Free with kfree().

vmalloc() allocates individual pages and maps them contiguously in the vmalloc address range. It suits large buffers that need no physical contiguity, such as module text or big tables, but costs page-table setup, TLB entries and whole-page rounding, and it may sleep, so treat it as process-context only. Because the pages are scattered, you cannot hand the buffer to a device as a single DMA address. kvmalloc() tries kmalloc first and falls back to vmalloc; free with kvfree().

GFP flags say what the allocator may do. GFP_KERNEL may sleep and perform direct reclaim, I/O and filesystem callbacks: the default in process context. GFP_ATOMIC never sleeps and may dip into reserves: for hardirq, softirq or spinlock-held code. GFP_NOWAIT also never sleeps but does not use reserves. GFP_NOIO/GFP_NOFS prevent recursion into block or filesystem code, though new code prefers memalloc_noio_save()/memalloc_nofs_save() scopes. Zone modifiers such as GFP_DMA32 restrict physical placement.
diagram:
kmalloc()          kmem_cache_alloc()          vmalloc()
     |                      |                       |
 kmalloc-8..8k        private cache                 |
 (> 8k: direct              |                       |
  to buddy)                 |                       |
     +----------+-----------+                       |
                |                                   |
         SLUB slab layer (per-CPU slabs)            |
                |                                   |
                v                                   v
   buddy allocator: alloc_pages(gfp, order)   order-0 pages
   physically contiguous, in the direct map   mapped into the
                                              vmalloc range
keypoints: kmalloc: physically contiguous, direct-mapped, rounded to a size class; large sizes go to the page allocator.
vmalloc: virtually contiguous only, may sleep, page-table/TLB overhead; free with vfree().
SLUB is the only slab allocator since 6.8; use kmem_cache_create() for hot fixed-size objects.
GFP_KERNEL may sleep; GFP_ATOMIC cannot and may use reserves; never GFP_KERNEL under a spinlock.
Buddy max order is typically 10 (4 MiB with 4 KiB pages); bigger contiguous buffers need CMA or boot-time reservation.

interview.q: Why not use vmalloc for everything?
interview.a: Each vmalloc allocation needs its own page-table entries in the vmalloc range, uses extra TLB entries because it cannot benefit from the huge pages of the direct map, rounds up to whole pages, and may sleep. It is not physically contiguous, so it is not directly DMA-able and virt_to_phys() is meaningless on it. For small objects kmalloc is faster and denser; vmalloc is for large, long-lived buffers.

interview.q: What happens if a GFP_ATOMIC allocation fails?
interview.a: It returns NULL quickly, having done no reclaim beyond waking kswapd. The caller must cope: drop the packet, retry later, defer to a workqueue that can allocate with GFP_KERNEL, or preallocate in advance. Network drivers refill RX rings with atomic allocations and simply retry on the next poll. Combining __GFP_NOFAIL with atomic context is not supported, because the allocator cannot reclaim there.

interview.q: How do you get a large physically contiguous buffer for a device?
interview.a: Use dma_alloc_coherent(), which on many platforms is backed by CMA, the Contiguous Memory Allocator: a region reserved at boot that the page allocator lends to movable pages and migrates on demand. Alternatively describe a reserved-memory region in the device tree and attach it to the device. High-order alloc_pages() at runtime often fails because physical memory becomes fragmented.

pitfalls: Calling kmalloc(GFP_KERNEL) or vmalloc() while holding a spinlock or in an interrupt handler.
Freeing vmalloc memory with kfree() or vice versa (kvfree() handles both).
Assuming kmalloc(n) uses exactly n bytes; it rounds to a size class (ksize() reports the usable size).

title: RX/TX path through the network stack
tldr: RX: driver, GRO, __netif_receive_skb_core, ip_rcv, routing, tcp_v4_rcv, socket queue. TX: tcp_sendmsg, ip_queue_xmit, neighbour, qdisc, ndo_start_xmit.
body: After NAPI hands an skb to napi_gro_receive(), GRO may merge it with earlier segments of the same flow. __netif_receive_skb_core() then runs, in order: generic XDP, VLAN tag extraction, packet taps (AF_PACKET, so tcpdump sees packets before netfilter), tc ingress, the netfilter ingress hook, delivery to VLAN devices, the device's rx_handler (bridge, bond, macvlan, which may consume the skb), and finally the protocol handler registered for skb->protocol, which for IPv4 is ip_rcv(). With RPS the skb may first be queued to another CPU's backlog.

ip_rcv() validates the header and traverses NF_INET_PRE_ROUTING (conntrack, DNAT). ip_rcv_finish() performs the route lookup, attaching a dst whose input function is ip_local_deliver() or ip_forward(). Local delivery reassembles fragments, passes NF_INET_LOCAL_IN and dispatches to tcp_v4_rcv(). TCP looks up the socket (established hash, then listeners); if no task owns the socket lock it processes the segment in softirq via tcp_rcv_established(), queues data on sk_receive_queue and calls sk_data_ready(), otherwise it appends to the socket backlog.

On TX, send() reaches tcp_sendmsg(), which copies user data into skbs on the write queue. tcp_write_xmit() sends what cwnd, the receive window and pacing allow; tcp_transmit_skb() clones the skb (the original stays for retransmission), builds the TCP header and calls ip_queue_xmit(). IP uses the socket's cached route, adds its header and passes NF_INET_LOCAL_OUT; ip_output() runs NF_INET_POST_ROUTING (SNAT), and ip_finish_output2() hands the packet to the neighbour layer.

neigh_output() prepends the cached hardware header or triggers ARP, then dev_queue_xmit() selects a TX queue and enqueues to its qdisc (kernel default pfifo_fast, often fq_codel via net.core.default_qdisc, under mq on multiqueue NICs). Dequeue calls dev_hard_start_xmit(), which applies software GSO or checksumming if the device lacks the feature and calls the driver's ndo_start_xmit(). The driver maps buffers for DMA, writes descriptors, rings the doorbell, and calls netif_stop_queue() when the ring is full; TX completion frees skbs and wakes the queue.
diagram:
RX                                TX
 NIC -> NAPI poll -> GRO           send() -> tcp_sendmsg()
 __netif_receive_skb_core()        tcp_write_xmit()
  XDP(gen), taps, tc, rx_handler   tcp_transmit_skb()
 ip_rcv        [PRE_ROUTING]       ip_queue_xmit  [LOCAL_OUT]
 ip_rcv_finish: route lookup       ip_output   [POST_ROUTING]
   +-> ip_forward  [FORWARD]       ip_finish_output2()
 ip_local_deliver [LOCAL_IN]       neigh_output() (ARP/hh)
 tcp_v4_rcv: socket lookup         dev_queue_xmit() -> qdisc
 tcp_rcv_established()             dev_hard_start_xmit()
 sk_receive_queue, wake reader     ndo_start_xmit() -> NIC
keypoints: tcpdump (AF_PACKET taps) sees RX packets before netfilter and TX packets just before the driver, after the qdisc.
The RX route lookup chooses local delivery or forwarding through dst->input.
TCP runs in softirq unless a task owns the socket lock, in which case the skb goes to the backlog.
TX: TCP clones skbs; IP traverses LOCAL_OUT and POST_ROUTING; the neighbour layer adds the L2 header; qdisc then driver.
Driver back-pressure: netif_stop_queue()/netif_wake_queue(), Byte Queue Limits and TCP Small Queues.

interview.q: Where can a received packet be dropped, and how do you find out?
interview.a: Many places: NIC ring overflow (ethtool -S missed or no-buffer counters), a full RPS backlog (/proc/net/softnet_stat), XDP or tc programs, netfilter rules, failed route lookup or rp_filter, bad checksums, or a full socket receive buffer (TCPRcvQDrop, UDP RcvbufErrors). Since 5.17 kfree_skb_reason() records a drop reason; perf on the skb:kfree_skb tracepoint, dropwatch or pwru pinpoints the location.

interview.q: Why does TCP processing sometimes happen in process context?
interview.a: If a task holds the socket lock, inside recvmsg() or sendmsg(), when the softirq arrives, the softirq must not touch socket state, so it appends the skb to the socket backlog. When the task calls release_sock(), it processes the backlog in its own context via sk_backlog_rcv(). This keeps locking light on the fast path while preserving segment order.

interview.q: What happens when the driver's TX ring fills up?
interview.a: The driver calls netif_stop_queue(), or netif_tx_stop_queue() for one queue, when it can no longer fit a maximally fragmented skb. Packets then wait in the qdisc, which drops on overflow, while TCP Small Queues limits how much each socket has below the TCP layer. On TX completion the driver frees descriptors and calls netif_wake_queue(). Returning NETDEV_TX_BUSY from ndo_start_xmit() is treated as a bug path.

pitfalls: Saying netfilter sees received packets before tcpdump does.
Forgetting that forwarded packets traverse PRE_ROUTING, FORWARD and POST_ROUTING but never LOCAL_IN or LOCAL_OUT.
Thinking TCP receive processing normally runs in the application's thread.

refs.t: Scaling in the Linux networking stack

title: Cross-compilation, toolchains & sysroot
tldr: A cross toolchain (binutils, compiler, libc, kernel headers) builds for the target; the sysroot supplies target headers and libraries; the kernel needs only ARCH and CROSS_COMPILE.
body: Cross-compiling means building on one machine for another architecture or ABI. In GNU terms, build is where you compile, host is where the result runs, and target matters only when building a compiler: it is what that compiler emits code for. A toolchain is binutils (as, ld, objcopy), GCC or Clang, a C library (glibc, musl or uClibc-ng) and the kernel UAPI headers that libc was built against, usually named by a tuple prefix such as aarch64-linux-gnu- or arm-linux-gnueabihf-.

The sysroot is a directory mirroring the target's /usr/include and library directories: the headers and libraries you compile and link against. --sysroot=DIR makes compiler and linker search there instead of the build machine's directories. Most cross-build breakage comes from host leakage: a configure script picks up /usr/include or the host's pkg-config. Set PKG_CONFIG_SYSROOT_DIR and PKG_CONFIG_LIBDIR, use a toolchain file for CMake (CMAKE_SYSROOT), and pass --host= to autotools.

The kernel needs no libc or sysroot: make ARCH=arm64 CROSS_COMPILE=aarch64-linux-gnu- defconfig Image dtbs modules. With Clang, make ARCH=arm64 LLVM=1 works because a single Clang binary targets every architecture. Out-of-tree modules must be built against the exact configured kernel tree (make -C $KDIR M=$PWD) with the same toolchain; vermagic and, with CONFIG_MODVERSIONS, symbol CRCs make the kernel reject mismatched modules.

The ABI must match the target user space. On arm32, hard-float (gnueabihf, floating-point arguments in VFP registers) and soft-float (gnueabi) binaries do not mix; glibc and musl binaries are not interchangeable; and a binary linked against newer glibc symbol versions fails with 'version GLIBC_2.34 not found'. glibc is also configured with a minimum kernel version and refuses to start on older kernels ('FATAL: kernel too old'). Check results with file and readelf -d/-A, and smoke-test with qemu-aarch64 -L SYSROOT.
diagram:
build machine (x86_64)              target board (arm64)
 +------------------------------+    +--------------------+
 | aarch64-linux-gnu-gcc        |    | /lib/ld-linux-     |
 | binutils: as, ld, objcopy    |    |   aarch64.so.1     |
 | --sysroot=$SYSROOT           |    | libc.so.6 (same    |
 | $SYSROOT/usr/include         | -> |   libc and ABI)    |
 | $SYSROOT/usr/lib: target     |    | your binary        |
 |   libc, libssl, ...          |    +--------------------+
 +------------------------------+

 kernel: make ARCH=arm64 CROSS_COMPILE=aarch64-linux-gnu-
         (or LLVM=1); no sysroot or libc needed
keypoints: Toolchain = binutils + compiler + libc + kernel UAPI headers, named by a tuple prefix.
Sysroot = target headers and libraries; --sysroot prevents host contamination.
Kernel: ARCH= and CROSS_COMPILE= (or LLVM=1); no sysroot needed.
ABI mismatches: hard vs soft float, glibc vs musl, glibc symbol versions, minimum kernel version.
Out-of-tree modules must match the kernel version, config and vermagic.

interview.q: A cross-compiled binary reports 'No such file or directory' although it exists. Why?
interview.a: The kernel cannot find the ELF interpreter named in PT_INTERP, for example /lib/ld-linux-aarch64.so.1 for a glibc binary on a musl root filesystem, or ld-linux-armhf.so.3 on a soft-float system, and execve() reports ENOENT. Check with readelf -l and file. Fix it by building against the target's libc and sysroot, or by linking statically.

interview.q: What does CROSS_COMPILE actually do in the kernel build?
interview.a: It is a prefix prepended to tool names: CC becomes $(CROSS_COMPILE)gcc, and likewise LD, OBJCOPY and the rest. ARCH selects arch/$(ARCH) for Kconfig, Makefiles and headers. Both must be passed consistently to every make invocation, including module builds and modules_install, or you configure for one architecture and build for another. With LLVM=1, clang and ld.lld are used with a target derived from ARCH.

interview.q: Why does an application need the target sysroot when the kernel does not?
interview.a: Applications include libc and third-party headers and link against shared libraries that must match those on the target, so the compiler needs the target's copies. The kernel is freestanding: it builds with -nostdinc and -ffreestanding, uses only its own headers, and links with its own linker script, so a cross compiler and binutils are all it needs.

pitfalls: Linking against the build machine's /usr/lib by accident (missing --sysroot or host pkg-config).
Mixing hard-float and soft-float objects or libraries on arm32.
Forgetting ARCH= on a later make step (menuconfig, modules_install) and silently reconfiguring for x86.

title: System call path (user to kernel)
tldr: A libc wrapper loads the syscall number and arguments into registers and traps; entry code saves pt_regs, dispatches to the sys_* handler, and returns a value or -errno.
body: User code calls a libc wrapper such as read(). On x86-64 the wrapper puts the syscall number in rax and arguments in rdi, rsi, rdx, r10, r8 and r9 (r10 replaces rcx, which the syscall instruction clobbers along with r11), then executes syscall. The CPU switches to ring 0 and jumps to the address in MSR_LSTAR, entry_SYSCALL_64. On arm64 the number goes in x8, arguments in x0 to x5, and svc #0 traps to EL1, reaching el0_svc().

The entry code switches to the task's kernel stack (on x86 also swapgs and, with PTI, a page-table switch), saves user registers into struct pt_regs, and calls C: do_syscall_64() on x86, invoke_syscall() on arm64. Common entry code runs seccomp, ptrace, tracepoint and audit hooks, then dispatches on the number to the sys_* handler, through sys_call_table or, on recent x86 kernels, a switch statement that avoids indirect branches. Handlers are written with SYSCALL_DEFINEn(), which generates wrappers that unpack arguments from pt_regs.

The handler accesses user memory only through copy_from_user()/copy_to_user() (SMAP on x86 and PAN on arm64 trap accidental direct access), does its work, possibly sleeping, and returns a long. On the way out the kernel handles pending work: signals, TIF_NEED_RESCHED and task work. It then restores registers and returns with sysretq (or iretq) on x86 or eret on arm64. Values from -4095 to -1 signal errors: the libc wrapper stores the negated value in errno and returns -1.

Some calls never enter the kernel: clock_gettime() and gettimeofday() are served by the vDSO, a kernel-provided shared object mapped into every process that reads time data from a shared page. A sleeping system call interrupted by a signal returns -ERESTARTSYS internally; depending on SA_RESTART the kernel restarts it transparently or returns EINTR. The legacy int $0x80 entry remains for 32-bit code, with the i386 syscall numbers and register convention.
diagram:
user:   read(fd, buf, n)                    (glibc wrapper)
         rax = 0 (__NR_read), rdi/rsi/rdx = args; syscall
 ---------------------------------------- ring 3 -> ring 0
 entry_SYSCALL_64: swapgs, kernel stack, save pt_regs
 do_syscall_64(regs, nr)
   entry hooks: seccomp, ptrace, audit, tracepoints
   dispatch nr -> __x64_sys_read(regs)
     ksys_read() -> vfs_read() -> f_op->read/read_iter
   exit work: signals, need_resched, task work
 sysretq (or iretq)
 ---------------------------------------- ring 0 -> ring 3
 glibc: ret in [-4095, -1] -> errno = -ret, return -1
keypoints: x86-64: number in rax, arguments in rdi, rsi, rdx, r10, r8, r9; syscall/sysret; entry_SYSCALL_64 -> do_syscall_64.
arm64: number in x8, arguments in x0-x5; svc #0 -> el0_svc -> invoke_syscall.
pt_regs is saved on the kernel stack; SYSCALL_DEFINEn wrappers unpack arguments from it.
The kernel returns -errno; libc maps -4095..-1 to errno and a -1 return.
The vDSO avoids the trap for clock_gettime/gettimeofday; -ERESTARTSYS plus SA_RESTART controls restarting.

interview.q: Why is r10 used instead of rcx for the fourth argument?
interview.a: The syscall instruction saves the user return address in rcx and RFLAGS in r11, overwriting both. So the kernel ABI moves the fourth argument to r10, unlike the normal function-call ABI, which uses rcx. Both rcx and r11 are clobbered across a system call, and libc wrappers declare them as such in their inline assembly.

interview.q: How do you add a new system call?
interview.a: Define it with SYSCALL_DEFINEn in the relevant subsystem, add it to the syscall tables (arch/x86/entry/syscalls/syscall_64.tbl, plus the generic table used by arm64 and RISC-V), declare it in include/linux/syscalls.h, and expose the number in the UAPI headers. Use fixed-size types and a flags argument for future extension, handle compat if needed, and add selftests and man-page text. Expect heavy review; an existing interface is often preferred.

interview.q: What does strace cost, and why?
interview.a: strace uses ptrace: the kernel stops the tracee at every system call entry and exit and switches to the tracer, which reads registers and memory with further system calls before resuming it. That adds several context switches per system call and can slow syscall-heavy programs dramatically. strace --seccomp-bpf limits stops to selected calls, and perf trace or bpftrace on the raw_syscalls tracepoints cost far less.

pitfalls: Calling library functions such as printf() system calls (printf buffers, then calls write()).
Thinking the kernel sets errno; the libc wrapper sets it from the negative return value.
Forgetting that vDSO calls never appear in strace.

title: Interrupts: hardirq, softirq, tasklet, threaded IRQ, workqueue
tldr: Do the minimum in the hard IRQ handler, then defer: softirqs or tasklets for fast atomic work, threaded IRQs or workqueues when the work must sleep.
body: A hardirq handler registered with request_irq() runs with local interrupts disabled. It cannot sleep, must be short, and returns IRQ_HANDLED, IRQ_NONE (not my device, which matters on shared lines) or IRQ_WAKE_THREAD. Typical work: read and acknowledge the device status, capture data that would otherwise be lost, and schedule deferred processing. Everything else belongs in a bottom half.

Softirqs are a fixed, compile-time set of ten vectors (HI, TIMER, NET_TX, NET_RX, BLOCK, IRQ_POLL, TASKLET, SCHED, HRTIMER, RCU). They run on IRQ exit, at local_bh_enable(), or in the per-CPU ksoftirqd thread under load. The same softirq can run on several CPUs at once, so its data must be per-CPU or locked. Tasklets are built on the HI and TASKLET softirqs, and one tasklet never runs on two CPUs simultaneously. Tasklets are deprecated; 6.9 added BH workqueues (WQ_BH) as their replacement.

Threaded IRQs, request_threaded_irq(irq, handler, thread_fn, flags, name, dev), run thread_fn in a dedicated irq/N-name kernel thread (SCHED_FIFO priority 50) that may sleep, which suits I2C- or SPI-attached devices. The primary handler returns IRQ_WAKE_THREAD. With a NULL primary handler you must pass IRQF_ONESHOT so the line stays masked until the thread finishes; otherwise a level-triggered interrupt would fire endlessly. The threadirqs boot option forces threading, and PREEMPT_RT does so for handlers not marked IRQF_NO_THREAD.

Workqueues run work items in process context on kworker threads: INIT_WORK(), then schedule_work() or queue_work() onto a queue from alloc_workqueue() with flags such as WQ_UNBOUND, WQ_HIGHPRI or WQ_MEM_RECLAIM (guarantees a rescuer thread for reclaim paths). Work items can sleep, take mutexes and allocate with GFP_KERNEL; queue_delayed_work() adds a timer. Always cancel_work_sync() or flush on teardown so a work item cannot run after its owner is freed.
diagram:
device raises IRQ
    |
 hardirq handler (local IRQs off, cannot sleep)
    |  ack device, grab volatile data, defer the rest
    +-------------------+--------------------+
    v                   v                    v
 softirq / tasklet   IRQ thread           workqueue
 atomic, no sleep;   irq/N-name kthread,  kworker, process
 same softirq may    SCHED_FIFO 50,       context, may sleep,
 run on many CPUs;   may sleep; ONESHOT   GFP_KERNEL ok,
 ksoftirqd if busy   keeps line masked    mutexes ok
keypoints: Hardirq: local IRQs disabled, cannot sleep; return IRQ_HANDLED, IRQ_NONE or IRQ_WAKE_THREAD.
Softirqs: 10 fixed vectors; the same vector may run concurrently on multiple CPUs; ksoftirqd takes over under load.
Tasklets are serialised per tasklet but deprecated in favour of BH workqueues (6.9+).
A threaded IRQ with a NULL primary handler requires IRQF_ONESHOT.
Workqueues run in process context, may sleep, and must be cancelled or flushed on teardown.

interview.q: When would you choose a threaded IRQ over a workqueue?
interview.a: A threaded IRQ is tied to the interrupt line: with IRQF_ONESHOT the core keeps the line masked until the thread finishes, the thread runs at RT priority, and the flow is explicit. It is the natural choice when acknowledging the interrupt needs a sleeping bus transfer, such as an I2C GPIO expander. A workqueue suits deferred work not tied to re-enabling the line, work that can be batched, or work queued from many sources.

interview.q: Can a softirq be preempted?
interview.a: On non-RT kernels a softirq runs with bottom halves disabled, so tasks cannot preempt it, but hard interrupts can interrupt it. If softirq processing runs too long or keeps re-raising, the remainder is handed to ksoftirqd, a normal-priority thread that competes with other tasks. On PREEMPT_RT softirqs run in task context, serialised by a per-CPU local lock, and are fully preemptible.

interview.q: How do you protect data shared between process context and a softirq?
interview.a: Use spin_lock_bh() in process context: it disables bottom halves locally, so the softirq cannot run on this CPU and spin on a lock its own CPU holds, while the lock excludes other CPUs. Inside the softirq a plain spin_lock() is enough, because softirqs do not preempt each other on the same CPU. If a hardirq handler also touches the data, use spin_lock_irqsave() everywhere it is taken outside that handler.

pitfalls: Calling sleeping functions (mutex_lock, msleep, GFP_KERNEL allocations, i2c_transfer) from a hardirq handler or tasklet.
Omitting IRQF_ONESHOT with a NULL primary handler (the request is rejected unless the irqchip is oneshot-safe), or returning IRQ_HANDLED on a shared line for an interrupt that is not yours.
Assuming a softirq never runs on two CPUs at once, or that tasklets give per-CPU parallelism.

title: TCP 3-way handshake, states & TIME_WAIT
tldr: The kernel completes SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK before accept() returns; close takes four segments, and the side that closes first holds TIME_WAIT for 60 seconds on Linux.
body: Active open: the client sends SYN with its initial sequence number and options (MSS, window scale, SACK-permitted, timestamps) and enters SYN_SENT. The listener replies SYN-ACK and records the half-open connection as a lightweight request sock in SYN_RECV, not a full socket. The client's ACK completes the handshake: the kernel creates the child socket in ESTABLISHED and puts it on the listener's accept queue, where accept() dequeues it. The whole handshake happens in the kernel, before the application calls accept().

Two limits matter. Half-open request socks are bounded by tcp_max_syn_backlog; under a SYN flood, SYN cookies (net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies=1 by default) encode connection state in the ISN so no state is stored. The accept queue is bounded by the listen() backlog, capped by net.core.somaxconn (4096 since 5.4). If the accept queue is full, the final ACK is dropped by default (tcp_abort_on_overflow=0) and the client retransmits. For listeners, ss -lnt shows the current accept queue as Recv-Q and its limit as Send-Q.

Close takes four segments because each direction shuts down independently. The active closer sends FIN (FIN_WAIT1), receives the ACK (FIN_WAIT2), then receives the peer's FIN, ACKs it and enters TIME_WAIT. The passive side moves to CLOSE_WAIT until its application calls close(), then LAST_ACK, then CLOSED. Simultaneous close passes through CLOSING. Piles of CLOSE_WAIT sockets mean an application that never closes its end; orphaned FIN_WAIT2 sockets are reaped after tcp_fin_timeout (60 s).

TIME_WAIT lasts 2*MSL, hardcoded to 60 seconds on Linux (TCP_TIMEWAIT_LEN). It lets the closer retransmit the final ACK if the peer's FIN is retransmitted, and stops delayed segments from an old connection being accepted by a new one with the same 4-tuple. Linux keeps it in a small inet_timewait_sock. tcp_tw_reuse lets outgoing connections reuse a TIME_WAIT 4-tuple when timestamps make it safe (default 2: loopback only). tcp_tw_recycle broke clients behind NAT and was removed in 4.12.
diagram:
client                              server
 CLOSED                              LISTEN
 SYN_SENT    --- SYN seq=x -------->  SYN_RECV (request sock)
 ESTABLISHED <-- SYN-ACK y, ack x+1 -
             --- ACK ack=y+1 ------>  ESTABLISHED, accept q
              ... data ...
 FIN_WAIT1   --- FIN -------------->  CLOSE_WAIT
 FIN_WAIT2   <-- ACK ---------------  (app calls close())
 TIME_WAIT   <-- FIN ---------------  LAST_ACK
 (60 s)      --- ACK -------------->  CLOSED
 CLOSED
keypoints: The handshake completes in the kernel; accept() only dequeues an established socket.
SYN queue (tcp_max_syn_backlog, SYN cookies) vs accept queue (listen backlog, somaxconn 4096 since 5.4).
The active closer gets TIME_WAIT (60 s on Linux); the passive side sits in CLOSE_WAIT until close().
TIME_WAIT protects against a lost final ACK and late duplicates from an old incarnation.
tcp_tw_reuse helps only outgoing connections; tcp_tw_recycle was removed in 4.12.

interview.q: A server shows thousands of TIME_WAIT sockets. Is that a problem?
interview.a: Usually not. TIME_WAIT sockets are small minisocks and harmless on a server accepting connections, since each client 4-tuple differs. They hurt a client opening many short connections to one destination, where they exhaust ephemeral ports (ip_local_port_range). Remedies: connection reuse or keepalive, a wider port range, tcp_tw_reuse for outgoing connections, or letting the other side close first. Avoid RST-on-close tricks with SO_LINGER 0.

interview.q: What does SO_REUSEADDR do on Linux, and how is SO_REUSEPORT different?
interview.a: SO_REUSEADDR lets bind() succeed on a local address and port still used by sockets in TIME_WAIT or other non-listening states, so a restarted server can rebind immediately. It does not let two sockets listen on the same port. SO_REUSEPORT, added in 3.9, does: several sockets bind and listen on one port, and the kernel spreads incoming connections across them by hash or by an attached BPF program.

interview.q: What happens when a SYN arrives for a port with no listener?
interview.a: TCP answers with an RST acknowledging the SYN, and the client's connect() fails with ECONNREFUSED. For UDP the equivalent is an ICMP port unreachable, which a connected UDP socket reports as ECONNREFUSED on a later call. If a firewall silently drops the SYN instead, the client retransmits with exponential backoff (tcp_syn_retries, default 6, about 127 seconds) and finally fails with ETIMEDOUT.

pitfalls: Saying the server always gets TIME_WAIT; it is whichever side closes first.
Recommending tcp_tw_recycle (removed) or claiming tcp_tw_reuse affects incoming connections.
Believing the Linux listen backlog counts half-open connections; it bounds the accept queue.

title: Buildroot vs Yocto
tldr: Both build a complete image from source; Buildroot is simple Kconfig and make producing a firmware image, Yocto is layered BitBake metadata producing packages, images and SDKs at scale.
body: Both build a complete embedded Linux system from source: cross toolchain (or an external one), boot loader, kernel, root filesystem and image files. Their philosophies differ. Buildroot is a set of Makefiles configured with Kconfig (make menuconfig) and aims for simplicity: one configuration produces one firmware image. The Yocto Project is an umbrella around OpenEmbedded and BitBake, a task executor that runs recipes; it aims to be a full distribution build system that scales to product lines.

A Buildroot package is a Config.in plus a .mk file using an infrastructure such as generic-package, autotools-package or cmake-package. Board customisation lives in a BR2_EXTERNAL tree: defconfigs, rootfs overlays, post-build scripts and patches. The output is a root filesystem image (ext4, squashfs, cpio) without a package manager on the target. Buildroot does not track configuration dependencies finely, so a toolchain or global option change generally means make clean all; make foo-rebuild rebuilds one package.

Yocto organises metadata into layers (meta-*): BSP layers define a MACHINE, distro layers set policy through DISTRO (Poky is the reference), and application layers add recipes. A recipe (.bb) runs tasks such as do_fetch, do_compile and do_install; .bbappend files modify another layer's recipe without forking it. The shared-state cache reuses task outputs keyed by input hashes, making incremental and team builds fast. Output includes packages (rpm, ipk or deb), images assembled from them, an SDK (populate_sdk) and license manifests.

Choose Buildroot for a single product, a small team, a minimal image and quick, easily understood builds. Choose Yocto when you maintain many machines or variants, depend on vendor BSP layers (most SoC vendors ship Yocto layers), need package feeds or per-package updates on target, SDKs for application developers, or rigorous license and CVE tracking. The costs are a steeper learning curve, tens of gigabytes of disk and long first builds; devtool eases modifying recipes and the kernel.
diagram:
Buildroot               Yocto / OE
 configuration   Kconfig (menuconfig)    layers + local.conf
 unit of work    Config.in + foo.mk      recipe .bb, .bbappend
 engine          make                    BitBake tasks
 incremental     limited, clean rebuilds sstate cache (hashes)
 target pkg mgr  none                    rpm / ipk / deb feeds
 SDK             make sdk (toolchain)    populate_sdk / eSDK
 customisation   BR2_EXTERNAL tree       own layer + bbappends
 learning curve  days                    weeks
keypoints: Buildroot: Kconfig + make, simple, image-oriented, no package manager on target.
Yocto: BitBake + layered metadata, recipes and bbappends, sstate cache, package feeds, SDKs.
Buildroot global configuration changes usually require a full rebuild.
Most SoC vendor BSPs ship as Yocto layers (e.g. meta-freescale, meta-ti).
Both support license reporting: Buildroot make legal-info, Yocto license manifests and SPDX.

interview.q: How do you add a custom application in each?
interview.a: Buildroot: create package/foo/Config.in and foo.mk in your BR2_EXTERNAL tree, set FOO_VERSION and FOO_SITE, use an infrastructure such as cmake-package or write the build and install commands, then enable BR2_PACKAGE_FOO. Yocto: write foo_1.0.bb in your layer with SRC_URI, LICENSE and LIC_FILES_CHKSUM, inherit cmake or define do_compile and do_install, and add foo to IMAGE_INSTALL in your image recipe.

interview.q: How do you patch the kernel in Yocto without forking the vendor layer?
interview.a: Create a bbappend for the kernel recipe in your own layer, for example linux-yocto_%.bbappend, prepend your files directory to FILESEXTRAPATHS, and add patches and config fragments to SRC_URI. devtool modify on the kernel recipe gives you a working git tree, and devtool finish writes your commits back into your layer as patches. Never edit the vendor layer in place.

interview.q: How do they support reproducible builds?
interview.a: Products must rebuild an identical image years later for fixes and audits. Both pin source versions and checksums and can archive all downloads (Buildroot's download directory and make source; Yocto's DL_DIR, own mirrors and the archiver class). Yocto tests for bit-for-bit reproducibility and sets SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH; Buildroot offers BR2_REPRODUCIBLE. Pinning layer revisions with repo manifests or kas, or Buildroot release tags, completes the picture.

pitfalls: Calling Yocto a distribution; it is a build system, and Poky is its reference distribution.
Expecting Buildroot to rebuild only affected packages after a toolchain or global option change.
Editing vendor layers directly instead of adding bbappends in your own layer.

title: volatile and memory barriers
tldr: volatile forces the compiler to perform every access but gives no atomicity and no CPU ordering; cross-CPU ordering needs paired barriers or acquire/release operations.
body: volatile tells the compiler that every access to the object is an observable side effect: it must perform each read and write as written, not cache the value in a register, not invent or remove accesses, and keep volatile accesses in program order relative to each other. It exists for memory-mapped device registers, volatile sig_atomic_t flags shared with signal handlers, and locals modified between setjmp() and longjmp().

What volatile does not do: make operations atomic (v++ is still load, add, store, so racing threads lose updates); emit CPU memory barriers, so a weakly ordered CPU such as ARM, POWER or RISC-V may still make the accesses visible to other cores in a different order; order volatile accesses against non-volatile ones; or synchronise threads under the C11 memory model, where a data race on a volatile object is still undefined behaviour. It also does nothing for cache coherency with DMA.

Ordering comes from barriers. barrier() is compiler-only: it prevents the compiler from moving memory accesses across it. mb(), rmb() and wmb() order all accesses, including MMIO; smp_mb(), smp_rmb() and smp_wmb() order accesses between CPUs and reduce to compiler barriers on uniprocessor builds; smp_store_release()/smp_load_acquire() give one-way ordering and are often cheaper. Barriers pair: a writer's smp_wmb() achieves nothing unless the reader has a matching smp_rmb() or acquire.

The kernel discourages volatile (see volatile considered harmful): shared data should be protected by locks, which already contain the necessary barriers, and deliberate lockless accesses use READ_ONCE()/WRITE_ONCE(). These are volatile accesses applied at the point of use: they prevent tearing (for aligned word-sized data), fusing and re-reading, but impose no CPU ordering. Device registers use readl()/writel(). In user space, C11 _Atomic with an explicit memory_order is the right tool.
diagram:
CPU0 (producer)                 CPU1 (consumer)
 data = 42;                      while (!READ_ONCE(flag))
 smp_wmb();      --pairs-->          cpu_relax();
 WRITE_ONCE(flag, 1);            smp_rmb();
                                 r = data;    /* 42 */

 release/acquire form:
 data = 42;                      if (smp_load_acquire(&flag))
 smp_store_release(&flag, 1);        r = data;    /* 42 */

 volatile alone: the compiler keeps both stores in order,
 but ARM/POWER may still make flag visible before data.
keypoints: volatile: the compiler must perform every access, in order relative to other volatile accesses.
Not atomic, no CPU barriers, no ordering against non-volatile accesses, not a thread synchronisation primitive.
barrier() = compiler only; smp_*() = inter-CPU ordering; mb/rmb/wmb also order MMIO.
Barriers must pair: wmb with rmb, release with acquire.
In the kernel use locks, READ_ONCE/WRITE_ONCE and readl/writel instead of volatile.

interview.q: Is volatile enough for a flag set by an ISR and polled in main() on a single-core MCU?
interview.a: Often, for a single naturally atomic variable: volatile forces the loop to re-read it, and a single core has no cross-CPU reordering. It is not enough if the flag guards other data the ISR wrote, because the compiler may move non-volatile accesses across it (add a compiler barrier), or if the variable is wider than the CPU's atomic access size, such as a 32-bit counter on an 8-bit AVR. Read-modify-write still needs interrupts masked.

interview.q: What does READ_ONCE() guarantee?
interview.a: A single, non-torn load of an aligned variable no larger than a machine word, which the compiler may not elide, fuse with other loads or repeat. Through address dependencies it also orders later dereferences of a loaded pointer. It does not order the load against other memory accesses at the CPU level; for that use smp_load_acquire() or explicit barriers. It also documents an intentional lockless access, which KCSAN understands.

interview.q: Why does a store-then-load pattern need smp_mb()?
interview.a: Store buffers let a CPU's later load complete before its earlier store becomes visible to others; this store-load reordering happens even on x86. If CPU0 runs x = 1; r0 = y and CPU1 runs y = 1; r1 = x, both can read 0. smp_wmb() and smp_rmb() do not order a store before a later load; only a full barrier does. The pattern appears in sleep/wakeup code, which is why set_current_state() includes a full barrier.

pitfalls: Claiming volatile makes i++ atomic or thread-safe.
Using smp_wmb() on the producer side without a paired read barrier or acquire on the consumer side.
Thinking x86 needs no barriers at all: it still reorders stores with later loads, and the compiler reorders freely.
