title: Undefined behaviour classics
tldr: Signed overflow, strict-aliasing violations, unsequenced modifications, bad shifts and NULL dereferences are undefined behaviour, and optimisers exploit the assumption that they never happen.
body: Undefined behaviour means the C standard imposes no requirements, and optimisers exploit that by assuming UB never occurs. Bugs then turn into surprising code: deleted checks, infinite loops, variables appearing to hold two values. Distinguish UB from unspecified behaviour, where one of several valid outcomes occurs (such as the order of evaluating function arguments), and implementation-defined behaviour, a documented choice (such as right-shifting a negative int, or whether plain char is signed).

Signed integer overflow is UB, while unsigned arithmetic wraps modulo 2^N. A compiler may therefore fold x + 1 > x to true for a signed x, or widen an int loop counter to 64 bits on the assumption that it never wraps. Check before the operation, or use __builtin_add_overflow() (kernel: check_add_overflow()). Shifting by a negative count or by at least the type's width is UB, as is left-shifting a negative value or shifting a 1 into the sign bit, so write 1U << 31. The kernel builds with -fno-strict-overflow, so signed arithmetic wraps there, but portable code cannot rely on that.

Strict aliasing: an object may only be accessed through an lvalue of its own compatible type, a signed or unsigned variant, or a character type. Reading a float through *(uint32_t *)&f is UB, and the compiler may reorder or cache loads assuming an int * and a float * never alias. Use memcpy(), which compiles to a simple move, or a union, which C permits for type punning. The kernel builds with -fno-strict-aliasing because it constantly reinterprets buffers, for example casting skb data to struct iphdr *.

Unsequenced modifications are UB: i = i++ + 1;, a[i] = i++; and f(i++, i++) modify, or read and modify, the same object without sequencing. C11 replaced 'sequence points' with sequenced-before, but &&, ||, ?:, the comma operator and the end of a full expression still sequence. Other classics are NULL or dangling pointer dereference, out-of-bounds access, reading uninitialised automatic variables, data races and modifying string literals. Catch them with UBSAN (-fsanitize=undefined, CONFIG_UBSAN), KASAN or ASan, and compiler warnings.
diagram:
/* tun driver, CVE-2009-1897 */
 struct sock *sk = tun->sk;  /* UB if tun is NULL ... */
 if (!tun)                   /* ... so GCC deleted this */
         return POLLERR;
 fix: reorder code; kernel adds
      -fno-delete-null-pointer-checks

 int x;    if (x + 1 < x) ...   /* check may vanish    */
 unsigned u = UINT_MAX; u + 1   /* defined: wraps to 0 */
 float f;  *(int *)&f           /* aliasing UB: memcpy */
 i = i++ + 1;                   /* unsequenced: UB     */
 1 << 31                        /* UB for int: use 1U  */
keypoints: UB lets the optimiser assume it never happens: bugs become deleted checks and strange code generation.
Signed overflow is UB, unsigned wraps; the kernel uses -fno-strict-overflow.
Strict aliasing: access via the object's own type or char; use memcpy or a union; the kernel uses -fno-strict-aliasing.
Unsequenced modifications (i = i++ + 1, f(i++, i++)) are UB; argument evaluation order is unspecified.
Shifts by >= width or negative counts, NULL dereference, out-of-bounds, uninitialised reads and data races are UB; use UBSAN/KASAN.

interview.q: How do you write a portable signed overflow check?
interview.a: Check before operating: for a + b with b > 0 test a > INT_MAX - b, and with b < 0 test a < INT_MIN - b. Simpler and clearer is __builtin_add_overflow(a, b, &res) in GCC and Clang, or in the kernel check_add_overflow() and the size_add()/array_size() helpers, which saturate allocation sizes so kmalloc fails instead of returning a short buffer. Never test a + b < a on signed types.

interview.q: Why does the kernel disable strict aliasing?
interview.a: Kernel code constantly reinterprets memory: casting skb data to struct iphdr, viewing page contents as different structures, type-punning in lockless code. Under strict aliasing these are UB, and the compiler could reorder or drop accesses, producing heisenbugs. Linus has long argued that the rule makes C unusable for low-level code, so Kbuild passes -fno-strict-aliasing and accepts slightly less optimisation for predictable semantics.

interview.q: Is plain char signed or unsigned?
interview.a: Implementation-defined: signed on x86, unsigned by default in the ARM, arm64, PowerPC and RISC-V ABIs. Code that compares a char with negative values or uses char as a small integer therefore behaves differently across architectures. Since 6.2 the kernel builds every architecture with -funsigned-char to remove that variation; use u8, s8 or an explicit signed char when the sign matters.

pitfalls: Saying signed overflow wraps in standard C.
Thinking UB only produces a garbage value at that line; it can change code before and after it.
Trying to fix aliasing problems with volatile instead of memcpy or a union.

title: Device model, platform drivers & probe
tldr: The driver core matches devices to drivers per bus; for non-discoverable SoC hardware the platform bus matches device tree compatible strings and calls probe().
body: The driver model rests on struct bus_type, struct device and struct device_driver, exposed in sysfs under /sys/bus, /sys/devices and /sys/class. When a device or driver registers, the bus's match() pairs them and the core calls the driver's probe(). Discoverable buses (PCI, USB) enumerate devices themselves. SoC peripherals are not discoverable, so firmware (device tree or ACPI) describes them and they are instantiated as platform_devices on the platform bus.

A platform_driver provides probe, remove and .driver.of_match_table, an array of struct of_device_id holding compatible strings; matching also tries ACPI IDs, an id_table, then the driver name. module_platform_driver() generates init and exit boilerplate, and MODULE_DEVICE_TABLE(of, ...) exports aliases so udev can autoload the module. In recent kernels remove returns void (the remove_new conversion), because a driver cannot refuse to be unbound.

In probe() you acquire resources: devm_platform_ioremap_resource() for registers, platform_get_irq() plus devm_request_irq(), devm_clk_get_enabled(), regulators, GPIOs and resets, then register with a subsystem such as net, input or IIO. devm_* resources are released automatically, in reverse order, on probe failure or unbind. If a dependency like a clock provider is not ready yet, return -EPROBE_DEFER and the core retries later; dev_err_probe() logs errors but stays quiet for deferral.

Binding can be forced or undone through the driver's bind and unbind files under /sys/bus/platform/drivers/, and /sys/kernel/debug/devices_deferred lists stuck probes with reasons. fw_devlink derives supplier-consumer links from DT phandles to order probing and avoid most deferral churn. Store driver data with platform_set_drvdata() and retrieve it in other callbacks with platform_get_drvdata() or dev_get_drvdata().
diagram:
DT node: compatible = "acme,foo-v2"
        |  of_platform_populate() at boot
        v
 struct platform_device ---+
                           |  platform_match():
 struct platform_driver ---+  of_match_table, ACPI,
   .of_match_table            id_table, then name
        |
        v
 really_probe() -> foo_probe(pdev)
   devm_platform_ioremap_resource(), platform_get_irq()
   devm_request_irq(), register with subsystem
   return 0 | -EPROBE_DEFER (retried later) | -errno
keypoints: Device model = bus_type + device + device_driver; bus match() then driver probe().
The platform bus handles non-discoverable devices described by DT or ACPI; DT matching uses compatible.
Use devm_* for automatic cleanup; return -EPROBE_DEFER when a dependency is not ready.
MODULE_DEVICE_TABLE(of, ...) enables module autoloading via uevent MODALIAS.
platform_driver.remove returns void in recent kernels.

interview.q: What is -EPROBE_DEFER and how does the core handle it?
interview.a: Probe returns it when a required resource such as a clock, regulator, GPIO or PHY has no provider yet. The core parks the device on a deferred list and retries deferred devices whenever another driver binds successfully, and again late in boot. dev_err_probe() records the reason, visible in /sys/kernel/debug/devices_deferred. fw_devlink reduces deferral by probing suppliers before their consumers.

interview.q: Why prefer devm_ APIs, and when are they dangerous?
interview.a: They tie resource lifetime to the driver binding, so error paths and remove() shrink and leaks disappear. The danger is ordering and lifetime: release happens in reverse order at unbind, not when the last user closes a file. A devm_request_irq() handler can fire after remove() has torn down state it uses, and devm_kzalloc() memory still referenced by an open character device is freed at unbind.

interview.q: How does a module get loaded automatically for a DT device?
interview.a: of_platform_populate() creates the platform_device, whose uevent carries a MODALIAS built from the node name, type and compatible strings (of:N...T...C...). MODULE_DEVICE_TABLE(of, ids) embeds matching aliases in the module, and depmod writes them to modules.alias. udev or mdev runs modprobe with that modalias, the module registers its platform_driver, and the core matches and probes the device.

pitfalls: Calling a manual free on a devm-managed resource, causing a double free at unbind.
Treating -EPROBE_DEFER as fatal and logging it loudly, or deferring forever on a resource that should be optional.
Touching hardware in module_init instead of in probe().

title: Sockets & epoll vs select/poll
tldr: select and poll rescan every descriptor on every call; epoll keeps the interest set in the kernel and returns only ready descriptors, in level- or edge-triggered mode.
body: A socket descriptor maps to a struct file whose private_data is a struct socket (the BSD layer, with proto_ops such as inet_stream_ops), which points to a struct sock holding protocol state, with sk->sk_prot set to tcp_prot for TCP. Readiness comes from the file's poll method, here sock_poll() calling tcp_poll(), which returns an event mask and registers the caller on the socket's wait queue. All three multiplexing APIs are built on that same callback.

select() takes three fd_set bitmaps, limited to descriptors below FD_SETSIZE (1024) in glibc; poll() takes an array of struct pollfd with no fixed limit. Both are stateless: every call copies the whole interest set into the kernel, invokes each file's poll to check readiness and add wait-queue entries, sleeps, and then rescans and copies results back. The cost is O(n) in watched descriptors per call regardless of how many are ready, and the application scans the results too.

epoll separates registration from waiting. epoll_create1() creates an eventpoll instance; epoll_ctl() with EPOLL_CTL_ADD, MOD or DEL registers a descriptor once, storing it in a red-black tree and hooking ep_poll_callback() into the file's wait queue. When the socket becomes ready, the callback moves the item to a ready list, and epoll_wait() just harvests that list, so the cost is O(ready). epoll is level-triggered by default: a descriptor is reported on every call while it remains readable.

EPOLLET (edge-triggered) reports only new readiness, so use non-blocking descriptors and read or write until EAGAIN, or you stall with data pending. EPOLLONESHOT disables a descriptor after one event until re-armed with EPOLL_CTL_MOD, which suits thread pools. EPOLLEXCLUSIVE avoids thundering-herd wakeups when many epoll instances watch one listening socket. epoll registers the open file description, not the descriptor number, so closing one of several duplicated descriptors does not remove the registration.
diagram:
select/poll (every call)        epoll
 +------------------------+      epoll_ctl(ADD, fd) once:
 | copy N fds into kernel |        rbtree item + callback on
 | f_op->poll() x N       |        the socket's wait queue
 | sleep on N wait queues |      data arrives:
 | rescan N, copy back    |        callback -> ready list
 +------------------------+      epoll_wait():
 cost O(N) per call                return ready items only
                                 cost O(ready)
keypoints: fd -> struct file -> struct socket (proto_ops) -> struct sock (sk_prot).
select: fd_set bitmap limited to FD_SETSIZE (1024); poll: pollfd array; both stateless and O(n).
epoll: interest set in the kernel (rbtree), ready list fed by a wait-queue callback; epoll_wait is O(ready).
Level-triggered by default; EPOLLET needs non-blocking fds and draining to EAGAIN.
epoll tracks open file descriptions; EPOLLEXCLUSIVE and EPOLLONESHOT help multi-threaded servers.

interview.q: When is select() or poll() still fine?
interview.a: With a small, dense set of descriptors, or when the set changes on almost every call, the O(n) cost is negligible and you avoid extra epoll_ctl() system calls. poll() is also portable across Unix systems, while epoll is Linux-specific (BSDs use kqueue). For tens of thousands of mostly idle connections, epoll's O(ready) behaviour wins clearly.

interview.q: Why must edge-triggered descriptors be non-blocking?
interview.a: With EPOLLET you are notified once when new data arrives. If you read only part of it, no further event comes until more data arrives, so you must loop until read() returns EAGAIN. With a blocking descriptor, the final read in that loop would block the entire event loop once the buffer is empty. The same applies to writes: write until EAGAIN, then wait for EPOLLOUT.

interview.q: What is the thundering-herd problem with accept()?
interview.a: Many processes waiting on the same listening socket all wake for one incoming connection; one wins accept() and the rest go back to sleep, wasting CPU. Blocking accept() has long used exclusive wakeups. With epoll, every instance watching the socket is woken unless it registered with EPOLLEXCLUSIVE (4.5+). SO_REUSEPORT goes further: each worker owns its own listening socket and the kernel distributes connections among them.

pitfalls: Claiming epoll is always faster; with a few descriptors the extra system calls can cost more.
Using EPOLLET with blocking sockets, or not draining to EAGAIN.
Assuming close(fd) always removes the registration; duplicated descriptors keep it alive.

title: Real-time Linux: PREEMPT_RT & latency
tldr: Real-time means bounded worst-case latency; PREEMPT_RT, mainline since 6.12, makes nearly all kernel code preemptible, but determinism also needs application and system tuning.
body: Real-time means bounded worst-case latency, not high throughput. PREEMPT_RT, merged into mainline in 6.12 (initially for x86, arm64 and RISC-V), makes almost all kernel code preemptible. spinlock_t and rwlock_t become rt_mutex-based sleeping locks with priority inheritance; interrupt handlers are forced into threads unless marked IRQF_NO_THREAD; softirqs run in task context; and local_lock_t replaces bare preemption disabling for per-CPU data. Only raw_spinlock_t sections and a few short regions remain non-preemptible.

Latency is the time from an event, such as an interrupt or timer expiry, to the RT task running. Contributors include interrupt-disabled and preemption-disabled sections, long raw-spinlock regions, firmware SMIs on x86, deep CPU idle states and frequency transitions, cache and TLB misses, page faults in the RT task, and priority inversion. A well-tuned PREEMPT_RT system typically achieves worst cases of tens of microseconds, while a non-RT kernel can reach milliseconds under load. Measure with cyclictest under stress, and attribute causes with rtla timerlat and rtla osnoise.

Application side: use SCHED_FIFO or SCHED_RR (priorities 1 to 99) or SCHED_DEADLINE; call mlockall(MCL_CURRENT | MCL_FUTURE) and pre-fault stacks and heap to avoid page faults; keep system calls with unbounded latency out of the RT loop; drive periodic loops with clock_nanosleep(CLOCK_MONOTONIC, TIMER_ABSTIME, ...); and use priority-inheritance mutexes (PTHREAD_PRIO_INHERIT) for shared locks. Set IRQ thread priorities (default SCHED_FIFO 50) deliberately relative to your tasks.

System side: isolate CPUs (isolcpus= or cpusets, nohz_full=, rcu_nocbs=), steer interrupts away with irqaffinity= and /proc/irq/*/smp_affinity, limit idle states (for example through /dev/cpu_dma_latency) and pin CPU frequency. RT throttling (sched_rt_runtime_us, 950 ms per second) and, in recent kernels, the fair deadline server keep a runaway RT task from starving everything else. Audit drivers for long raw-spinlock or IRQ-off sections.
diagram:
event (device IRQ / timer expiry)
   |<-- IRQ latency: IRQs-off sections, SMIs, idle exit
 hardirq entry -> wake IRQ thread or expire hrtimer
   |<-- scheduling latency: preempt-off, raw spinlocks
 scheduler picks the highest-priority RT task
   |<-- context switch, cache/TLB refill
 RT task runs        total = what cyclictest reports

 measure: cyclictest, rtla timerlat/osnoise, ftrace
 tune:    isolcpus, nohz_full, irqaffinity, mlockall
keypoints: Real-time = bounded worst-case latency; PREEMPT_RT has been mainline since 6.12.
spinlock_t/rwlock_t become sleeping PI locks on RT; raw_spinlock_t still spins.
Forced threaded IRQs (SCHED_FIFO 50 by default) and softirqs in task context.
Measure the maximum, not the average: cyclictest under load, rtla timerlat/osnoise.
App: SCHED_FIFO, mlockall, pre-faulting, PI mutexes, absolute-time sleeps; system: CPU isolation, IRQ affinity, idle/frequency control.

interview.q: What changes for driver writers on PREEMPT_RT?
interview.a: spin_lock_irqsave() no longer disables interrupts and may sleep, so spinlock_t cannot be used in truly atomic contexts: IRQF_NO_THREAD handlers, inside raw_spinlock or preempt_disable() sections. Allocating memory with interrupts disabled or under a raw spinlock is forbidden. Use local_lock for per-CPU data instead of preempt_disable(). Code needing true atomicity, such as irqchips and clockevents, must use raw_spinlock_t and keep those sections short.

interview.q: Why does PREEMPT_RT reduce throughput?
interview.a: Sleeping locks cost more than spinning ones (extra context switches and priority-inheritance bookkeeping), threaded interrupts add a wakeup and context switch per interrupt, softirq work in threads batches less, and more preemption points mean more scheduling overhead. RT optimises the worst case at the expense of the average. That is the right trade for many control systems, while servers typically use voluntary or dynamic preemption.

interview.q: What does cyclictest measure?
interview.a: It runs threads at RT priority that sleep until an absolute time with clock_nanosleep() and records how late they wake: the combined timer interrupt, scheduling and context-switch latency. Run it for hours under realistic stress (stress-ng, network and storage load) with memory locked, and look at the maximum and the histogram, not the average. rtla timerlat breaks latency into IRQ and thread components and can auto-trace when a threshold is exceeded.

pitfalls: Equating real-time with fast.
Benchmarking average latency, or running cyclictest on an idle system.
Assuming PREEMPT_RT alone delivers determinism without tuning firmware/SMIs, idle states, IRQ affinity and the application.

title: Endianness & network byte order
tldr: Endianness is the byte order of multi-byte values in memory; network protocols are big-endian, most Linux CPUs are little-endian, so convert explicitly at every boundary.
body: Endianness is the order of bytes of a multi-byte value in memory. Little-endian stores the least significant byte at the lowest address: x86, and in practice most ARM, arm64 and RISC-V Linux systems. Big-endian stores the most significant byte first: network protocols, s390, older PowerPC and some MIPS and network processors. ARM and PowerPC cores are bi-endian, but a given kernel and user space run in one mode, and ppc64le is now common. Bit order within a byte is not addressable, so it is unaffected.

Network byte order is big-endian. User space converts with htons(), htonl(), ntohs() and ntohl(), or with htobe32(), le32toh() and friends from endian.h. The kernel uses cpu_to_be32(), be16_to_cpu(), cpu_to_le32() and so on, and annotates storage with __be32 and __le16; sparse (make C=1) warns when they are mixed with plain integers. On a CPU of matching endianness the conversions compile to nothing; otherwise to a byte-swap instruction such as bswap or rev.

Hardware has its own byte order. PCI and most SoC peripherals are little-endian, which is why readl()/writel() assume little-endian and swap on big-endian CPUs; use ioread32be() for big-endian devices. Storage formats specify it too: ext4 metadata is little-endian. Endianness bugs hide on x86 and surface when code runs on a big-endian target, or when a multi-byte field is read from a byte buffer by casting instead of with get_unaligned_be32(), which also handles alignment.

Bitfields are worse: the order in which fields are allocated within a storage unit is implementation-defined and in practice follows endianness, so they are unsafe for wire formats. The kernel's struct iphdr uses __LITTLE_ENDIAN_BITFIELD to declare ihl and version in swapped order. Prefer masks and shifts on a correctly converted integer. To detect byte order at compile time use __BYTE_ORDER__ (GCC and Clang) or the kernel's __BIG_ENDIAN/__LITTLE_ENDIAN macros.
diagram:
uint32_t v = 0x12345678;   stored at address A

 address:         A      A+1    A+2    A+3
 little-endian:  0x78   0x56   0x34   0x12   (x86, arm64)
 big-endian:     0x12   0x34   0x56   0x78   (network order)

 send:    hdr->len = htonl(len);       /* cpu -> be32 */
 receive: len = ntohl(hdr->len);       /* be32 -> cpu */
 kernel:  __be32 x = cpu_to_be32(v);   v = be32_to_cpu(x);
 parse:   v = get_unaligned_be32(buf); /* any alignment */
keypoints: Little-endian: least significant byte at the lowest address; network byte order is big-endian.
htons/htonl/ntohs/ntohl; kernel cpu_to_be32/be32_to_cpu with __be32/__le32 types checked by sparse.
Conversions are no-ops on a matching CPU and a single swap instruction otherwise.
readl/writel assume little-endian devices; use the *be accessors for big-endian devices.
Never use bitfields or raw pointer casts for wire formats; use masks and get_unaligned_be*().

interview.q: How do you detect endianness at runtime, and why might you not need to?
interview.a: Store a known multi-byte value and inspect its first byte: with uint16_t x = 1, the system is little-endian if *(uint8_t *)&x == 1, which is allowed because character types may alias anything. But code should not branch on endianness at all: write conversions that are correct everywhere, such as assembling bytes with shifts, ((uint32_t)b[0] << 24) | ..., or be32toh()/be32_to_cpu(), which compile optimally for the host.

interview.q: Does endianness affect single-byte or string fields?
interview.a: No. Byte order applies only to multi-byte scalars; strings and byte arrays are sequences of individual bytes and look identical on every CPU. In an Ethernet header, the MAC addresses (byte arrays) need no conversion but the 16-bit EtherType does: skb->protocol is stored as __be16 and compared with htons(ETH_P_IP).

interview.q: What breaks when a driver written on x86 runs on a big-endian CPU?
interview.a: Mostly descriptor and buffer fields that the device reads or writes by DMA: the device expects little-endian, but the CPU stores big-endian values, so the fields must be declared __le32 and filled with cpu_to_le32(). MMIO through readl()/writel() usually still works, while bitfield-based register definitions break. Such missing conversions are invisible on x86, which is why running sparse with endian annotations matters.

pitfalls: Saying ARM is big-endian; Linux on ARM and arm64 is almost always little-endian.
Converting twice (ntohl() on a value already in host order) or omitting conversions that happen to be no-ops on x86.
Parsing protocol headers with bitfields and expecting portability.

title: Kernel debugging: printk, dynamic debug, ftrace, oops, kgdb
tldr: Log with leveled printk and runtime-switchable dynamic debug, trace with ftrace, decode oopses with faddr2line, and use kgdb, sanitizers and kdump for the hard cases.
body: printk() writes to the kernel log buffer with a level from KERN_EMERG to KERN_DEBUG; prefer pr_err(), dev_err() or netdev_err() so messages carry device context, and *_ratelimited() in hot paths. The console prints only messages more severe than console_loglevel (/proc/sys/kernel/printk, loglevel=), while dmesg reads everything. With CONFIG_DYNAMIC_DEBUG, every pr_debug()/dev_dbg() site can be enabled at runtime by writing, for example, module foo +p to /sys/kernel/debug/dynamic_debug/control, or with foo.dyndbg=+p at boot.

ftrace lives in tracefs at /sys/kernel/tracing. The function tracer logs kernel function calls; function_graph shows call trees with durations; set_ftrace_filter and set_graph_function narrow the scope. Static tracepoints (sched:sched_switch, irq:*, net:*, skb:kfree_skb) are cheap and stable. Latency tracers (irqsoff, preemptoff, wakeup_rt) find long non-preemptible sections. trace_printk() is a fast debug print into the trace buffer, and trace-cmd, perf and bpftrace front-end the same infrastructure.

An oops is the kernel's report of an unexpected exception: a reason line such as 'BUG: kernel NULL pointer dereference', CPU, PID and command, taint flags, registers and a call trace. RIP: 0010:foo_read+0x2c/0x90 [foo] means 0x2c bytes into the 0x90-byte function foo_read in module foo. Map it to a source line with scripts/faddr2line foo.ko foo_read+0x2c/0x90, or pipe the whole log through scripts/decode_stacktrace.sh vmlinux. A small fault address usually means a NULL struct pointer plus a member offset.

For interactive debugging build with CONFIG_KGDB and CONFIG_KGDB_SERIAL_CONSOLE, boot with kgdboc=ttyS0,115200 kgdbwait, and attach gdb vmlinux using target remote on the serial port; under QEMU use its built-in gdbstub (-s -S). JTAG via OpenOCD covers early boot. Sanitizers catch whole bug classes: KASAN (memory errors), KCSAN (data races), UBSAN, lockdep (CONFIG_PROVE_LOCKING) and kmemleak. Post-mortem, kdump captures a vmcore for the crash utility, and pstore/ramoops preserves logs across reboots on embedded boards.
diagram:
BUG: kernel NULL pointer dereference, address: 0000...0010
 Oops: 0000 [#1] PREEMPT SMP
 CPU: 2 PID: 431 Comm: cat Tainted: G           O
 RIP: 0010:foo_read+0x2c/0x90 [foo]
           ^^^^^^^^ ^^^^ ^^^^  ^^^
           function off  size  module
 Call Trace:
  vfs_read+0xb5/0x1c0
  ksys_read+0x67/0xf0
  do_syscall_64+0x5d/0x170

 $ scripts/faddr2line foo.ko foo_read+0x2c/0x90
 foo_read at drivers/misc/foo.c:142
keypoints: Use pr_*/dev_* with levels; pr_debug/dev_dbg sites toggle at runtime via dynamic debug.
ftrace via /sys/kernel/tracing: function, function_graph, tracepoints, latency tracers.
Oops 'func+off/size [module]' -> faddr2line or decode_stacktrace.sh with the exact matching build.
kgdb over serial (kgdboc) or the QEMU gdbstub; JTAG for early boot.
Sanitizers: KASAN, KCSAN, UBSAN, lockdep, kmemleak; kdump and pstore for post-mortem analysis.

interview.q: What is the difference between an oops and a panic?
interview.a: An oops is an exception report: the kernel kills the offending task and tries to continue, now tainted, unless panic_on_oops=1. An oops in interrupt context, or one that kills the idle task or init, escalates to a panic. A panic stops the system, or reboots after panic=N seconds. BUG() triggers an oops deliberately, while WARN() prints a backtrace and continues.

interview.q: How would you find out why a kernel function is slow?
interview.a: Use the function_graph tracer with set_graph_function to get per-call durations of the function and its children, or an fentry/kprobe tool such as bcc's funclatency for a latency histogram. For sporadic spikes, enable sched_switch and irq tracepoints to see what preempted or blocked it, or use the irqsoff and preemptoff tracers and rtla osnoise/timerlat. perf record -g gives a statistical CPU profile.

interview.q: What do taint flags such as 'G O' mean?
interview.a: Taint records conditions that make a bug report less trustworthy. 'P' means a proprietary module was loaded and 'G' that all modules are GPL-compatible; 'O' an out-of-tree module, 'E' an unsigned module, 'W' an earlier warning, 'D' an earlier oops. /proc/sys/kernel/tainted shows the bitmask. Upstream developers often ask for a reproduction on an untainted kernel.

pitfalls: Decoding an oops against a vmlinux or module built from different sources or configuration.
Leaving heavy printk in hot paths, which floods the log and changes timing; prefer tracepoints or trace_printk().
Debugging a later cascading oops instead of the first one in the log.

title: Offloads (TSO/GSO/GRO, checksum), zero-copy & XDP/eBPF
tldr: Offloads move large super-packets through the stack, zero-copy avoids user-kernel copies, and XDP runs eBPF in the driver before an skb even exists.
body: Per-packet overhead, not byte count, dominates stack cost, so Linux moves large super-packets through the stack. TSO lets the NIC cut one large TCP skb (64 KiB, or more with BIG TCP) into MSS-sized segments. GSO does the same in software just before the driver, in validate_xmit_skb(), so even devices without TSO get one stack traversal per large skb. GRO is the receive side: napi_gro_receive() merges consecutive segments of a flow before the stack sees them. LRO is a hardware equivalent, but it loses header details and must be off when forwarding.

Checksum offload is described by skb->ip_summed. On TX, CHECKSUM_PARTIAL means the stack has seeded the pseudo-header sum, and csum_start/csum_offset tell the NIC where to complete it. On RX, CHECKSUM_UNNECESSARY means the hardware verified it; CHECKSUM_COMPLETE means the hardware supplied a raw ones'-complement sum in skb->csum, which the stack adjusts as headers are pulled; CHECKSUM_NONE means software must verify. Capabilities are NETIF_F_* feature bits, toggled with ethtool -K.

Copies between user and kernel are the other large cost. sendfile() and splice() attach page-cache pages to socket skbs as fragments. MSG_ZEROCOPY, after enabling SO_ZEROCOPY, pins user pages for send(); completions arrive on the socket error queue and the buffer must not be reused before then, so it pays off only for large writes. On receive, options include TCP_ZEROCOPY_RECEIVE with mmap, io_uring zero-copy receive in recent kernels, and AF_XDP sockets that share a UMEM area with the driver.

XDP runs an eBPF program in the driver's NAPI poll on the raw buffer, before any skb is allocated. It returns XDP_DROP, XDP_PASS (continue into the stack), XDP_TX (bounce out of the same NIC), XDP_REDIRECT (another NIC, a CPU via cpumap, or an AF_XDP socket) or XDP_ABORTED. Modes are native (driver support), generic (skb-based fallback, slow) and offloaded (some SmartNICs). Programs pass the verifier, are JIT-compiled and share state through BPF maps; tc BPF (tcx since 6.6) covers skb-level ingress and egress.
diagram:
TX: 64 KiB TCP skb --GSO (software) / TSO (NIC)--> MSS segs
 RX:
 NIC -> driver NAPI poll --XDP prog--> DROP / TX / REDIRECT
                            |            (other NIC, cpumap,
                            | PASS        AF_XDP socket)
                            v
                 build skb (napi_build_skb)
                            |
                 GRO: merge segments of a flow
                            |
          __netif_receive_skb_core -> tc/tcx BPF -> IP
keypoints: TSO = hardware segmentation; GSO = software segmentation as late as possible; GRO = software RX coalescing; LRO breaks forwarding.
ip_summed: CHECKSUM_PARTIAL on TX; CHECKSUM_UNNECESSARY, COMPLETE or NONE on RX.
MSG_ZEROCOPY needs SO_ZEROCOPY and completion handling via the error queue.
XDP runs before skb allocation; actions DROP, PASS, TX, REDIRECT, ABORTED.
eBPF: verifier, JIT, maps; tc/tcx for skb-level hooks.

interview.q: Why must LRO be off on a router or bridge, while GRO is fine?
interview.a: LRO merges packets in hardware and discards per-segment header detail, so the merged packet cannot be re-segmented exactly as received; forwarding it would change what goes on the wire. GRO keeps enough metadata (gso_size, gso_type) for GSO to re-segment on output with the original boundaries. The kernel disables LRO automatically when forwarding is enabled on a device or the device joins a bridge.

interview.q: When does XDP beat the regular stack, and what are its limits?
interview.a: It wins for early drop such as DDoS filtering, for load balancing and for simple forwarding, avoiding skb allocation, GRO and the stack, reaching millions of packets per second per core. Limits: programs must pass the verifier, there is no access to socket or full stack state, multi-buffer (jumbo) support depends on the driver, and native mode needs driver support. Anything needing TCP state belongs at the tc or socket layer.

interview.q: Why does tcpdump show packets far larger than the MTU?
interview.a: Because the capture tap sits above GSO/TSO on transmit and after GRO on receive, it sees the super-packets, while the wire carries normal MSS-sized segments. To see on-wire packets, disable offloads with ethtool -K eth0 tso off gso off gro off on a test machine, or capture from a mirror port. Bad checksums on outgoing packets in captures are a similar artefact of checksum offload.

pitfalls: Thinking GSO requires hardware support.
Assuming XDP_PASS packets bypass GRO or netfilter; they enter the normal stack.
Reusing a MSG_ZEROCOPY buffer before its completion notification arrives.

title: Power management: runtime PM, suspend/resume
tldr: System sleep suspends everything through phased dev_pm_ops callbacks; runtime PM powers down individual idle devices using usage counts and autosuspend.
body: Linux device power management has two frameworks. System sleep suspends the whole machine when mem or disk is written to /sys/power/state. The mem state maps to suspend-to-idle (s2idle), standby (shallow) or suspend-to-RAM (deep), as selected in /sys/power/mem_sleep; hibernation (disk) writes an image to swap and powers off. Runtime PM powers down individual idle devices while the system runs. CPU idle states and frequency scaling are separate subsystems (cpuidle, cpufreq).

Suspend sequence: sync filesystems, freeze user tasks and freezable kernel threads, then run device callbacks in phases, prepare, suspend, suspend_late and suspend_noirq, children before parents. Then non-boot CPUs go offline (not for s2idle) and the platform enters its sleep state (PSCI SYSTEM_SUSPEND on arm64, ACPI S3 on x86). Resume runs the mirror phases, resume_noirq, resume_early, resume and complete, parents first. Drivers provide callbacks in struct dev_pm_ops, e.g. with DEFINE_SIMPLE_DEV_PM_OPS() and pm_sleep_ptr().

Runtime PM is reference counted. A driver calls pm_runtime_enable() in probe; before touching hardware it calls pm_runtime_resume_and_get(), which unlike pm_runtime_get_sync() drops the usage count on failure; afterwards it calls pm_runtime_mark_last_busy() and pm_runtime_put_autosuspend(). When the usage count and the count of active children reach zero, the core calls runtime_suspend after the autosuspend delay, and the next get calls runtime_resume. Parents stay active while children are active, and generic PM domains (genpd) power off a domain once all its devices are suspended.

For wakeup, device_init_wakeup(dev, true) declares a wakeup-capable device, enable_irq_wake() keeps its interrupt armed during suspend, and wakeup sources (pm_wakeup_event()) block suspend while events are being processed. Common bugs: touching registers of a runtime-suspended device (bus faults, or reads of all ones), unbalanced get/put counts, failing to restore registers lost in power-off, and interrupt handlers running while the device is suspended. /sys/kernel/debug/wakeup_sources and /sys/power/pm_test help debugging.
diagram:
echo mem > /sys/power/state
 (mem_sleep selects s2idle | shallow | deep)
   |
 sync filesystems, freeze tasks
   |
 devices: prepare -> suspend -> suspend_late -> suspend_noirq
          (children before parents)
   |
 non-boot CPUs offline (not for s2idle), syscore suspend
   |
 platform sleep: PSCI SYSTEM_SUSPEND / ACPI S3 ... wake IRQ
   |
 resume_noirq -> resume_early -> resume -> complete
          (parents before children), thaw tasks
keypoints: System sleep: s2idle, shallow (standby), deep (suspend-to-RAM), disk (hibernate); /sys/power/state + mem_sleep.
dev_pm_ops phases: prepare, suspend, suspend_late, suspend_noirq, and the mirror resume phases.
Runtime PM: usage count + autosuspend; pm_runtime_resume_and_get() and pm_runtime_put_autosuspend().
Wakeup: device_init_wakeup(), enable_irq_wake(), wakeup sources.
genpd powers off a domain when all member devices are runtime-suspended.

interview.q: Why prefer pm_runtime_resume_and_get() over pm_runtime_get_sync()?
interview.a: pm_runtime_get_sync() increments the usage count even when resume fails, so every error path must call pm_runtime_put_noidle(); many drivers forgot, leaking the count and keeping the device powered forever. pm_runtime_resume_and_get() drops the count itself on failure and returns a negative errno, which allows the simple 'if (ret) return ret;' pattern.

interview.q: What is the noirq phase for?
interview.a: suspend_noirq runs after the core has disabled device interrupt handlers, so the driver cannot be surprised by its own interrupt while putting the hardware into its final low-power state. It is used for the last register saves and by bus types such as PCI to set device power states. Interrupts marked with enable_irq_wake() stay armed for wakeup. resume_noirq restores state before handlers are re-enabled.

interview.q: How do runtime PM and system suspend interact?
interview.a: If a device is already runtime-suspended at system suspend, the driver can often leave it that way; flags such as DPM_FLAG_SMART_SUSPEND let the core skip redundant callbacks, and pm_runtime_force_suspend()/pm_runtime_force_resume() can serve as system-sleep callbacks to reuse the runtime paths. The core takes a runtime-PM reference in the prepare phase and disables runtime PM before suspend_late, so drivers must not rely on runtime PM transitions during system suspend.

pitfalls: Leaking runtime PM usage counts through pm_runtime_get_sync() error paths.
Accessing registers of a suspended device from an IRQ handler, debugfs or a workqueue.
Confusing cpuidle/cpufreq with device runtime PM.

title: container_of and intrusive lists (list_head)
tldr: container_of() recovers the enclosing struct from a pointer to an embedded member, which makes embedded list_head, work_struct and struct device the kernel's form of object orientation.
body: container_of(ptr, type, member) converts a pointer to a member back to a pointer to the enclosing structure by subtracting the member's offset, essentially (type *)((char *)ptr - offsetof(type, member)). The kernel macro adds a compile-time type check, a static_assert using __same_type(), so passing a pointer of the wrong type fails to build. It costs one subtraction, or nothing when the member is first. container_of_const() preserves const-ness.

This enables the kernel's object-oriented style through embedding rather than pointers: a driver struct embeds struct device, struct cdev, struct work_struct, struct kref or struct list_head, and callbacks receive a pointer to the embedded member. A work handler receives struct work_struct *work and recovers its context with container_of(work, struct foo, work); helpers such as to_platform_device() are thin wrappers around it. Embedding means one allocation, no extra pointer chase, and a lifetime tied to the outer object.

struct list_head { struct list_head *next, *prev; } forms an intrusive, circular, doubly linked list. The head is a sentinel list_head (LIST_HEAD(name) or INIT_LIST_HEAD()) that points to itself when the list is empty, and elements embed a list_head member. list_add() inserts after the head (stack order), list_add_tail() before it (queue order), list_del() unlinks in O(1) given the element, and list_for_each_entry(pos, head, member) iterates using container_of. One object can be on several lists through several members.

Deleting while iterating requires list_for_each_entry_safe(), which caches the next element. list_del() sets the entry's pointers to LIST_POISON1/LIST_POISON2 so use-after-delete faults recognisably; list_del_init() leaves the entry re-addable and testable with list_empty(). Hash tables use hlist_head, a single pointer per bucket, halving bucket memory. Lists provide no locking: protect them with a lock, or use the RCU variants such as list_add_rcu() and list_for_each_entry_rcu() for lockless readers.
diagram:
struct foo { int id; struct list_head node; char name[16]; };

   head <--> A.node <--> B.node <--> C.node <--> (head)
   sentinel head, circular; empty when head.next == &head

 struct foo A:
   +--------+-----------------+-----------------+
   | id     | node.next/prev  | name[16]        |
   +--------+-----------------+-----------------+
   ^ &A     ^ &A.node
   |<------>|  offsetof(struct foo, node) = 8 on 64-bit

 container_of(&A.node, struct foo, node) == &A
keypoints: container_of = member pointer minus offsetof(type, member), with a compile-time type check.
Embedding (struct device, work_struct, kref, list_head) plus container_of is the kernel's OOP.
list_head: circular, doubly linked, sentinel head; list_add (LIFO) vs list_add_tail (FIFO).
Use list_for_each_entry_safe() when deleting during iteration.
No built-in locking; hlist for hash buckets; _rcu variants for lockless readers.

interview.q: Why does the kernel prefer intrusive lists to a generic list of void pointers?
interview.a: No separate node allocation, so insertion cannot fail with -ENOMEM and works in atomic context; better cache locality; O(1) removal given the object, without searching; type safety through container_of instead of void * casts; and an object can sit on several lists at once through several embedded nodes. The cost is that the struct must declare in advance which lists it can join.

interview.q: What does list_for_each_entry() expand to, roughly?
interview.a: for (pos = list_first_entry(head, typeof(*pos), member); !list_entry_is_head(pos, head, member); pos = list_next_entry(pos, member)). list_first_entry() is container_of(head->next, ...). The loop ends when pos maps back to the head, so after a loop that finds nothing, pos is a bogus pointer computed from the head; using the cursor after the loop is a known bug class that a 2022 cleanup targeted.

interview.q: How would you write container_of without the type check, and what is the danger?
interview.a: #define container_of(p, T, m) ((T *)((char *)(p) - offsetof(T, m))). Casting to char * makes the subtraction byte-granular. Without the check, passing a pointer to a different member, or to a member of another struct type, compiles silently and yields a pointer into the wrong place, which means memory corruption. The kernel version asserts that the pointer's type matches the member's type, or is void *.

pitfalls: Deleting entries inside list_for_each_entry() instead of the _safe variant.
Using the loop cursor after a list_for_each_entry() that did not break.
Assuming list_head operations are thread-safe.
